The table presented is an excerpt from Chapter 3 (“Input Description”) of the TALPA 2D Finite Elements in Geotechnical Engineering manual (Service Pack 2025-4 Build 146). It catalogues the input records that TALPA recognizes, together with section numbers and page references. The table is organized into four logical columns:

1. Record identifier (e.g. “3.5.9”)
2. Record name (e.g. “FIRE”)
3. Brief description or full title of the record (e.g. “Analysis of temperature dependent material behavior/material degradation for concrete and steel materials”)
4. Manual page number where full details may be found (e.g. “3-13”)

Entries run from 3.5.9 through 3.21, and include both general finite-element controls and specific CSG (Construction Stage Manager) commands. Key groups of records include:

• Material and behavior controls (Sections 3.5.9–3.5.14)  
  – 3.5.9 FIRE: Fire and temperature-dependent degradation for concrete/steel  
  – 3.5.10 CONC: Concrete material controls  
  – 3.5.11 TSTF: Steel-concrete bond behavior (tension stiffening)  
  – 3.5.12 GRAN: Control of material law GRAN  
  – 3.5.13 MSTE: Material algorithm control  
  – 3.5.14 DEFO: Storage of nodal displacements  

• Load, sequence and solver controls (3.5.15–3.5.18)  
  – 3.5.15 LSEQ: Load case sequences (defining order of load application)  
  – 3.5.16 AFIX: Kinematic degree-of-freedom constraints  
  – 3.5.17 SOLV: Equation solver selection and settings  
  – 3.5.18 CORE: Parallel computation control  

• Phreatic surfaces and primary loads (3.6–3.8)  
  – 3.6 PHRS: Definition of phreatic (groundwater) surfaces  
  – 3.7 PLC: Primary load case (initial stress state)  
  – 3.8 TPLC: Primary load case temperature  

• Element grouping, load cases and copies (3.9–3.12)  
  – 3.9 GRP: Definition and control of element groups  
  – 3.10 LC: Load case definition  
  – 3.11 LCC: Copying or cloning existing load cases  
  – 3.12 HIST: Iteration history monitoring  

• Limit-state and general system characteristics (3.13–3.15)  
  – 3.13 NSTR: Control of material limit-state evaluations  
  – 3.14 CSYS: General system characteristics for CSG mode  
  – 3.15 CCRL: Control parameters for analysis in CSG mode  

• CSG-specific records (3.16–3.20)  
  – 3.16 CS: Construction stages definitions  
  – 3.17 CGRP: Element group controls per stage  
  – 3.18 CLOA: Load reference for stage-based loading  
  – 3.19 CGW: Global groundwater level control across stages  
  – 3.20 CTXT: Arbitrary text annotations in CSG mode  

• Output extent control (3.21)  
  – 3.21 ECHO: Master switch for output extent in CSG mode  
     • 3.21.1 Element results  
     • 3.21.2 Averaged element results at nodes  
     • 3.21.3 Distributed support reactions  
     • 3.21.4 Residual forces  
     • 3.21.5 Material point statistics  
     • 3.21.6 Cross-sectional stress distribution plots (fiber beams)  

Each record name is a literal keyword that must appear in TALPA’s free-format text input to activate the corresponding functionality. Page references guide the user to detailed syntax, parameter lists and examples. This structured catalog is essential for automated parsing and indexing within a RAG-enabled vector store, enabling rapid lookup of where and how each keyword is employed in the TALPA manual.

CSG The Construction Stage Manager Geotechnics allows for automatic generation of the analysis sequence, based on an intuitive description of the construction stages.. FEA Finite Element Analysis - actual calculation of the analysis steps (construction stages) by means of the Finite Element Method..
 1.1 Construction Stage Manager (CSG)
 Executed in mode CSG, TALPA supports the automatic generation of a analysis sequence, based on an intuitive description of the single construction stages. The actual calculation is then executed in mode FEA.
 Description of the construction stages is based on element groups and the philosophy that only changes in relation to the previous construction stage (e.g. installation, removal, change of properties of element groups) are specified. Groups that remain unchanged (and therefore are based on the foregoing construction stage), are treated automatically.
 In CSG-mode input records CSYS, CCRL, CS, CGRP, CLOA, CGW and ECHO are evaluated.
 Finite Element Analysis (FEA)
 In FEA mode TALPA allows for linear or non-linear analysis of stresses and deformations both for
 arbitrary shaped plane structures that are loaded in-plane (plane stress or plane strain conditions)
 •
 and axisymmetric three-dimensional structures
 by means of the finite element method. The main focus of TALPA is the numerical analysis of geotechnical related taks and soil mechanics.
 The analysis requires a descretized system (splitting of the structure into an assembly of indi- vidual elements interconnected at nodes) that is stored in the data base. TALPA features the following element types:
 planar continuum elements
 • beam elements
 spring/ interface elements
 cable elements
 truss elements
 All element types offer various optional nonlinear effects, allowing for an effective and realistic capturing of relevant mechanical effects regarding the structure’s load carrying characteris- tics. This involves in particular interaction between soil and structural members including wall- friction and nonlinear load carrying characteristics of soil. Other important aspects, to name a
 few, are load transfer via (grouted) anchors, load redistribution capabilities of geo-grids, yield- ing/ tensile failure of struts, formation of plastic hinges and nonlinear load carrying behavior of (reinforced) concrete members.
 The program handles structures with rigid or elastic types of support. Elastic support can be provided linearly distributed or point-wise. Additionally, rigid elements or skew supports can be taken into account.

Additionally, rigid elements or skew supports can be taken into account..
 TALPA calculates the effects of nodal, line, block and temperature loads. The program con- tains special capabilities for the generation of loads from construction stages or primary stress states.
 The program supports numerous non-linear material models (e.g. elastoplastic, viscoplastic). Accounting for non-linear support effects, such as friction or slip, is possible, as well.
 Program control is essentially done via a free format text input file, allowing for parametrized input and supporting various data generation capabilities (CADINP scripting language).
 Essential computational results are strictly stored in the data base and are therefore accessible, e.g. for graphical postprocessing. he output includes the nodal deformations, the stresses at the centroids of elements and nodes and the reaction forces additional to the input.
 The analysis of nonlinear systems is a demanding engineering task. The increased sensitivity of these systems puts a high demand on modeling issues. Moreover, particular characteristics of the finite element solution procedure are likely to become evident. Therefore, it is generally advisable to increase the analysis model’s complexity gradually. Hence, as a rule, prior to running a nonlinear analysis, system and loads should be validated by a plain linear analysis.
 Engineering assessment of the computed results is indispensable.

This black-and-white line drawing (Figure 2.1) shows a simple, right-handed planar Cartesian coordinate system in the X–Y plane, with emphasis on the sign convention for in-plane rotations about the out-of-plane Z-axis. The key graphic elements are:

1. Axes  
   - A thick horizontal line represents the X-axis. It extends well beyond the intersection point in both left and right directions, but only the right-hand end is terminated by an arrowhead, indicating the positive X direction.  
   - A similarly thick vertical line represents the Y-axis. It crosses the horizontal line at a right angle (the origin) and extends both slightly above and much farther below that intersection. Only the bottom end carries an arrowhead, marking the positive Y direction.  
   - The origin itself is implied by the precise intersection of the two solid lines; no special marker (dot or circle) is drawn at that point.

2. Axis Labeling  
   - The vertical arrow is labeled “y” just to the left of the downward-pointing arrowhead.  
   - The horizontal arrow receives no letter in the visible portion of this excerpt, but context makes clear it is the X-axis.

3. Positive-Rotation Indicator  
   - Between the positive X-axis (to the right) and the positive Y-axis (downward) sits a dotted circular arc. This arc sweeps in a clockwise sense from the X-axis toward the Y-axis.  
   - A small arrowhead at the end of the dashed curve (adjacent to the vertical line) underscores that the direction of this arc is the “positive” rotational sense.  
   - Midway along the arc is the Greek label “φ_z,” denoting the rotation angle about the Z-axis.

4. Caption  
   - Centered below the graphic is the caption “Figure 2.1: Planar coordinate system,” anchoring the drawing in a document or report.

Taken together, the figure visually reinforces the additional text’s statement that (a) plane systems lie entirely in the X–Y plane, (b) the Cartesian frame is right-handed, and (c) positive rotations about the Z-axis are defined by a clockwise sweep of the X-axis into the Y-axis when viewed from the positive Z direction. No out-of-plane loadings or gridlines are shown; the focus remains strictly on the axes, their orientation, and the sign convention for in-plane rotations.

Plane systems are located in the plane spanned by the X- and Y-axes of a cartesian coordinate system. This system is right-handed; a positive rotation is therefore defined by a clockwise rotation of X about the Z-axis (view corresponds to positive Z-direction). Plane systems are
 loaded in-plane, exclusively.

TALPA supports three basic analysis models:
 The total strain normal to the structure’s plane is zero. The thickness of the planar elements defaults to 1.0 m. Orientation of the coordinate system can be chosen arbitrarily; however, it is common practice to have the global Y-direction aligned with the gravity direction.
 This model allows for the analysis of axisymmetric structures under axisymmetric loads. In this case, the mesh represents a meridional section, rotating about the X axis. The analysis is based on a circular element spanning an angle of 1 rad. Essential characteristics of the axisymmetric analysis model are:
 – The appearance of a circular strain.
 – Supports in Y-direction are not a necessary condition for a kinematically stable system.
 – The dimension of nodal loads is no longer kN, instead kN/m circumference is used. Line loads change from kN/m to kN/m2 and bedding constants from kN/m2 to kN/m3.
 – Beam elements cannot be used together with axisymmetric elements.
 The stresses perpendicular to the structure’s plane are zero (e.g. building walls). Orienta- tion of the coordinate system can be chosen arbitrarily; however, it is common practice to have the global Y-direction aligned with the gravity direction. Friction materials (soil materi- als) are not a valid option for this model.

Truss and cable elements can only transmit axial forces. In order to restrict the cable reaction to tensile force transfer, a nonlinear analysis is required.
 Optional nonlinear effects are:
 • Initial slip (GAP)
 • Tensile failure upon reaching tensile rupture force (CRAC)
 • Yielding (YIEL)
 • Reaction according to a specified material work law (AQUA: SSLA).
 Hint
 When simulating a loading history using primary states, the following should be consid- ered:
 GAP is related to the total deformation of the element.
 CRAC Straining beyond the element’s tensile strength yields to an immediate drop of the tensile capacity to zero. This damage cannot be recovered, tensile forces are no longer transfered by the element – even after a complete load reversal. Continuing loading yields crack growth. Compression cannot be transfered unless the crack has closed completely, i.e. the total deformation must become negative.

The image is titled “Figure 2.2: Standard nonlinear spring response curves.”  It consists of three adjacent, piece-wise‐linear plots of principal spring force (vertical axis, labeled P with an upward arrow) versus principal displacement (horizontal axis, labeled V with a rightward arrow).  A dashed, vertical reference line marks zero displacement in each plot.  Each sub-plot illustrates one of the three optional nonlinear behaviors that can be superimposed on the basic linear spring law P = C·Δ (Eq. 2.1):

1. Left sub-plot (Initial slip – “GAP”):  
   - For small positive or negative displacements around zero, the force remains zero (a horizontal segment), indicating a free gap before contact.  On the horizontal axis, small double-headed arrows and the label “GAP” bracket the zero‐force zone on both the tension (right) and compression (left) sides.  
   - Once the displacement exceeds the opening or closing gap, the curve transitions into a straight line through the origin’s offset, with slope C (the spring constant).  This line represents engagement of the spring after initial slip.  

2. Center sub-plot (Tensile rupture – “RISS” or “CRAC”):  
   - Starting from large negative displacement (left), a straight line with positive slope C rises toward the origin, passing through zero displacement.  Beyond zero, the line continues upward until it reaches a peak force, marked by a small vertical drop labeled “RISS” on the left of the drop.  
   - At that point the force instantaneously falls (vertical line segment) to a lower residual level (often zero), representing sudden tensile failure or crack opening.  Beyond the drop, the curve may continue with a reduced or zero stiffness, indicating that the spring no longer carries full load in tension.  

3. Right sub-plot (Yielding – “+YIEL”):  
   - A straight, elastic line with slope C extends from negative displacements through zero up to the yield point.  
   - At the yield force level a horizontal plateau appears (force held constant at the yield value, indicated by the label “+YIEL” next to the flat segment).  This models plastic flow or slip at constant force.  
   - After the plateau, the curve may resume a stiffer slope (strain‐hardening branch), shown as a second inclined line beyond the yield plateau.

The figure presents a schematic of a 2D rigid‐frictional interface element in its undeformed (unloaded) configuration. Visually, the element is rendered as two perfectly parallel horizontal lines, each terminating in small, filled circular markers that denote the four nodal points of the element. The lower line connects nodes “1” and “2” (left to right), while the upper, coincident line connects nodes “1′” and “2′.” Together these four nodes define a zero-thickness quadrilateral: the top edge (between 1′ and 2′) is the frictional interface proper, and the bottom edge (between 1 and 2) is its “back” or secondary edge.  

Along the middle of the element – roughly halfway between the two lines – two small red diamonds are placed symmetrically, one closer to the left half and one to the right. These symbols typically represent internal integration or Gauss points used in the numerical formulation to capture shear and normal stress distributions across the interface.  

Superimposed on the element is a local Cartesian coordinate system:  
 • A red arrow labeled “X” originates at the element’s centroid and points vertically upward, indicating the positive normal direction (perpendicular to the interface edge). This local x‐axis governs the axial (opening/compression) behavior of the interface.  
 • A green arrow labeled “Y” is drawn horizontally and points toward the left, indicating the positive tangential or shear direction along the interface edge.  

Node labeling and numbering follow a consistent convention: node 1 at the lower‐left corner, node 2 at the lower‐right; node 1′ immediately above node 1, node 2′ immediately above node 2. The interface edge is formed by the top two nodes (1′–2′), which lie on the side where contact conditions are enforced. The opposite edge (1–2) bounds the interfacing half‐space or soil/structure region.  

Because the element is shown in its unloaded state, the two parallel lines coincide in projection (zero thickness), but in a real model a reference thickness H can be prescribed to relate the element’s stiffness back to realistic material properties. In practice, very high initial stiffness values—either user‐defined or derived from the Young’s and shear moduli of an associated bedding material—are assigned so that the interface behaves quasi‐rigidly until slip or separation occurs. If no explicit H is provided, the solver automatically computes a small finite thickness that ensures numerical stability while preserving the zero‐thickness kinematic idealization.  

Overall, this drawing succinctly communicates:  
1. The quadrilateral, four‐node topology of a 2D interface element.  
2. The designation of the interface edge (nodes 1′–2′) versus the opposing edge (nodes 1–2).  
3. The local coordinate system, with x normal to the interface and y tangential.  
4. Placement of internal integration points (red diamonds) for shear/normal stress evaluation.  

This element is widely used in geotechnical finite‐element models for soil–structure interaction, layered soil interfaces, sliding surfaces in slopes, and other scenarios where contact with frictional behavior must be represented.

The image (labeled “Figure 2.4: Axial and shear deformation of 2D interface elements”) consists of two schematic side-by-side diagrams, each representing a single 2D rigid-frictional interface element in its deformed configuration. Both sketches share the same node numbering convention and local coordinate axes, but the left one illustrates primarily axial (opening/compression) deformation, while the right one highlights pure shear deformation.

Common features in both diagrams:

  • Nodes  
    – Lower edge: node “1” at the left, node “2” at the right (solid circles).  
    – Upper edge: node “1′” above node 1, node “2′” above node 2 (open circles).  
  • Local coordinate system  
    – A red arrow labeled “x” points vertically upward, indicating the local normal (axial) direction of the interface.  
    – A green arrow labeled “Y” (or “y,” depending on the diagram’s labeling) points horizontally to the left, indicating the local tangential (shear) direction.  
  • Interface midline  
    – A thin dotted line connects the midpoints of the top and bottom edges; this represents the idealized zero-thickness interface before deformation.  

Left diagram (axial opening/compression plus slight shear):  
  – The bottom edge remains horizontal between nodes 1 and 2.  
  – The top edge between nodes 1′ and 2′ is sloped upward from left (1′) to right (2′), indicating a rigid rotation of the upper segment.  
  – Two small red diamonds are placed along the interface midline to mark sample integration or contact points.  
  – A bracketed vertical arrow labeled “Δu” on the right side spanning from the bottom node 2 up to the top node 2′ quantifies the normal (axial) displacement.  
  – The green shear arrow along the bottom edge points leftward, implying a negative tangential slip component, although the main highlighted deformation here is the opening Δu.  

Right diagram (pure shear):  
  – Both top and bottom edges remain parallel and horizontal—no vertical separation is drawn.  
  – The entire top edge has translated horizontally relative to the bottom edge. Node 1′ has shifted leftward compared with node 1.  
  – Only a single red diamond appears along the midline, emphasizing the shear sampling point.  
  – The red vertical “x” and green horizontal “Y” arrows are reproduced for reference but there is no Δu bracket, since the focus is on tangential displacement.  
  – The green arrow along the mid-section again indicates the direction of positive shear slip (here leftward).  

Interpretation in the context of rigid‐frictional interface modeling:  
  – In the local x-direction the element can open (tensile failure) or close (unlimited compressive transfer).  
  – In the local y-direction it follows an elastoplastic Coulomb law, resisting shear until slip.  
  – These zero-thickness line elements connect two mechanical regions (soil layers, structural surfaces, slip surfaces) by enforcing very high initial stiffness normal to the interface, while allowing controlled shear transfer.  
  – Node pairs (1–1′ and 2–2′) form the quadrilateral element, and their relative rigid translations/rotations produce the illustrated axial and shear deformations.

Rigid Frictional Interface elements can be used to simulate the contact conditions between two mechanically interacting bodies of a model. Common use cases in geotechnics include soil- structure interaction, modeling of the interface between distinct soil layers, the slip surface of an unstable slope etc.
 2D interface elements topologically consist of four nodes and are characterized by a very small thickness to length ratio, being ideally zero-thickness elements in the unloaded configuration. Therefore, two edges are formed, with the edge defined between the first two nodes being the interface edge, which lies on the side where the interface is defined. The local coordinate system is defined with local x-axis perpendicular to the interface edge and pointing towards the opposite edge (Fig. 2.3). 2D Rigid Frictional Interfaces can be generated along a structural line with the use of record SOFIMSHC: SLNS and option TYPE INTF.
 Rigid Frictional Interface elements are characterized by two distinct actions: an axial one, along local x-axis, and a shear one, along local y-axis (Fig. 2.4). Their material properties can be defined with the use of record AQUA: BMAT. The initial stiffness of interface elements is ex- pected to be very high, compared to the surrounding elements, in order to ensure an initial rigid connectivity between the two regions. Instead of explicitly defining stiffness constants, the elements may derive their stiffness by the Young’s and Shear Moduli of the material associ- ated with the bedding properties. This is possible by defining a reference thickness H, which corresponds to the finite thickness of the physical matter that the interface elements represent, despite their zero (or other) thickness on the generated mesh. An additional reduction of the shear strength may be applied, with the use of the corresponding factor RFAC.
 Hint
 If parameter H is not provided, then an appropriate finite material thickness is calculated internally, which will provide quasi-rigid but numerically robust interface elements. The automatic determination of interface material thickness is recommended.

The SOFiSTiK default ansatz for a 2D continuum element is based on the concept of enhanced assumed strains (EAS). The essential characteristics of this ansatz are shortly motivated and described in the following.
 Geometry of the plain element is topologically described by 4 nodes in the element corner points (QUAD). The standard ansatz space of a corresponding isoparametric element formu- lation using bilinear ansatz functions provides for relatively limited kinematics of the element, only. As an important consequence, a tendency towards ’locking’ can be observed for elements of this type. The well-known example of a QUAD element subjected to centric planar uniaxial bending illustrates this behavior. The element’s bilinear function space for the displacements is not able to reproduce the bending kinematics accurately - resulting in parasitic (unphysical) shear strains that induce a significant artifical stiffening of the element’s response. This effect is commonly known as (shear) ’locking’.
 To alleviate this problem, normally a strong refinement of the element discretization is required. Alternative, more efficient, options to overcome the phenomenon are
 a) a sufficient increase of the order of the element ansatz space (=more degrees of freedom per element), e.g., using ansatz functions for the displacements of quadratic, cubic and higher order;
 •
 b) an element technological, internal enhancement of the element kinematics.
 Methods falling in class b), have received great attention also adressing the issue of efficient shell element formulations. This triggered the development of numerous strategies for element enhancement.
 The basic idea of the EAS concept is based on the notion that parasitic strains are responsible for the observed locking effects. As a consequence, the EAS directly aims at enhancing the
 ansatz space for the strains by terms that are not directly induced by the ansatz for the dis- placements (assumed). This is done in such a way that the parasitic strains, possibly induced by the insufficient ansatz space for the displacements, are compensated (eliminated) by the assumed strains...

This is done in such a way that the parasitic strains, possibly induced by the insufficient ansatz space for the displacements, are compensated (eliminated) by the assumed strains....
 It can be shown that it is permissible to derive an element local formulation of the assumed strains - provided that certain constraints are considered (Simo and Hughes [1] and Simo and Rifai [2]). The essential benefit is: Elimination of the additional degrees of freedom corrspond- ing to the enhanced terms already on element level, i.e., they do not add to the global number of system unknowns (→ efficiency)!
 Further benefits:
 • Choice of element ansatz not required until computation; no remeshing required in case of changes.
 • MPC’s (multi point constraints) that allow, e.g., for consistent connection between quadratic and linear elements, are not required.
 • In contrast to many other approaches for element enhancement, adoption of the EAS con- cept in a nonlinear framework is rather straight forward and can be achieved with minor overhead, only.
 The well established Wilson/Taylor element with so called "incompatible modes" is a special case of the more general EAS concept (Simo and Rifai [2]).
 Optionally, the EAS ansatz can be suppressed via CTRL option QART 0. In this case, element behavior is controlled by isoparametric bilinear ansatz functions.
 The non-conforming types are suppressed in the case of triangular elements. For general load- ing states these elements are of very limited use since they show a strong tendency towards shear-locking - resulting in a far too stiff prediction of the system response. The adoption of this element for the analysis of general type problems is discouraged.
 For additional reading regarding this topic see, e.g., Bischoff [3] or Klinkel and Wagner [4].
 Various state-of-the-art nonlinear continuum material laws are available. For details, please refer to the AQUA manual AQUA: NMAT.

The image is a schematic 2-D depiction of a single quadrilateral finite element under uniaxial compression, intended to illustrate the concept of nodal balance of forces in a “primary state.” Visually, it consists of a grey‐filled square with a bold black border, representing the element domain. At the four corner nodes of this square three distinct sets of arrows convey stresses and forces:

 1. Central Stress Vector (red)  
    - A vertical double‐headed red arrow is drawn at the center of the square, pointing both upward and downward.  
    - This arrow symbolizes the element’s internal compressive stress state that has already been reached and is being carried over into the primary state.  

 2. Internal Nodal Forces (green)

Caption: “Figure 2.6: Initial stress state transfer: balance of forces.” This diagram concretely visualizes how a previously established (primary) stress and force state is adopted for the next analysis step in nonlinear finite‐element procedures—ensuring proper accounting of loading history, equilibrium, and potential response under modified boundary conditions.

Primary states (primary load cases) are frequently used in nonlinear analyses, in particular they are the standard means for the numerical simulation of staged construction processes. To this end, an already reached system state is adopted as primary state for the directly succeeding computation step (construction stage).
 Moreover, the load carrying behavior of soils is often characterized by pronounced nonlinear reactions, which also introduces a certain sensitivity with respect to the loading history. For example, for the current reaction it makes a difference, wether previous unloading has been encountered or not. Also here, the adoption of primary states helps to adequately simulate the relevant loading history.
 The basic concept of primary states is subsequently illustrated ba means of a finite element subjected to uniaxial compression.
 • We assume, that a (compressive) element stress state is given (red).
 • Then, inherent internal nodal forces (=expansive forces) are obtained via integration of the stresses over the element domain (green).
 • Balance of forces: If external nodal loads (blue) of same magnitude counteract the internal nodal forces at each node of the element, the element is in a state of equilibrium.
 Adoption of a primary state for the current computation step is readily illustrated in continuation of the example above. First, transfer of stresses from the referenced primary state is accom- plished along with the corresponding internal nodal forces (FACL). The following scenarios are obtained:
 a) For the current computation step, the same external loads apply as for the referenced primary state. Balance of forces then yields a resulting force vector with zero magnitude (assuming, the referenced primary state represents a state of equilibrium). The element is in a state of equilibrium, no further deformation/ change of stress evolves.
 b) Currently applied external loading has changed in comparison to the referenced primary state. The resulting force is no longer of zero magnitude. In consequence, a change of deformation/ stress state will occur.
 c) No external loading in the current computation step is applied, e.g., due to deactivation of adjacent elements and consequential loss of nodal reset forces. Then, the resulting force on the element emerges from the internal force state, only. The element expands, in case of free deformability and elastic material behavior it will reattain its unstrained initial position.

c) No external loading in the current computation step is applied, e.g., due to deactivation of adjacent elements and consequential loss of nodal reset forces. Then, the resulting force on the element emerges from the internal force state, only. The element expands, in case of free deformability and elastic material behavior it will reattain its unstrained initial position..
 This scenario is merely a special case of scenario b).
 The same observations apply for a complex finite element model. If some elements are re- moved from a primary state configuration - including the corresponding loads - the original equilibrium is disturbed and unbalanced forces emerge at the boundary nodes of the removed parts.
 In real problems either part only of the loading is used, or the primary state is reduced (relax- ation, stiffness reduction method), or parts of the system are removed, replaced or modified regarding their stiffness. In all cases, corresponding unbalanced forces evolve, initiating load- ing or unloading response of the structure. In order to cover all situations encountered in practice, TALPA features flexible and element group specific options for control of the various scenarios (see record GRP).

 While the historical loading history of the soil is unknown to a large extent, the description of the current state is usually obtained based on the soil’s bulk density and the lateral earth pressure coefficient K . Soil is a porous material consisting of solid particles which together represent the grain skele- ton. The pores can be filled with fluid (commonly water) and air. Hence we talk about soil as a three phase system (Figure 2.10).
 For quasi-saturated soils, an explicit consideration of the air volume V (Figure 2.10b) can be neglected and a corresponding 2-phase approach can be established. The 2-phase model explicitly accounts for (excess) pore water pressure p and effective stress σ′ acting on the grain skeleton. It relies on Terzagi’s principle of effective stresses
 σ = σ′ + p ,
 (2.15)
 where σ denotes the total stress. Combining this with the assumption of undrained conditions, i.e. flow of pore water is prevented, a relation between volumetric change and change of pore water pressure can be derived. Together, this facilitates a differentiated simulation of the evolution of pore water pressure and effective stress. Details of the model are given in (AQUA: NMAT, TYPE UNDR).
 The 2-phase model is activated by assigning undrained or drained conditions via the group control GRP TYPE UNDR/ DRAI.
 When undrained material parameters are defined and the undrained analysis is activated (cf. GRP TYPE) the stiffness of the pore water is automatically added to the stiffness of the soil skeleton.
 Distinction is then made between the effective stresses Δσ′ and pore pressures Δσ, which are saved separately in the data base.
 The second part of the Terzaghi’s principle states that all quantifiable effects of the changes in soil stresses (e.g. volume changes, shape changes, shear resistance) are a direct conse- quence of a change in effective stresses σ′. As a repercussion of this statement, the non-linear soil analysis according to the method described in this subsection is based solely on the ef- fective stresses σ′ and the effective strength (e.g. φ′, c’) and stiffness parameters (e.g. E′ , ν′).

As a consequence NC soil under undrained conditions experience increase in the pore water pressure under shear. The pore pressure Δp monotonically increases with the increase of the axial deformation ε and the increase of the deviatoric stress q (Figures 2.11a and 2.12a). The effective stress path in p − q diagram (Fig. 2.12) shows that the mean effective stress p′ is reduced during the loading stage and the undrained strength is smaller than the drained strength.

On the other hand, the undrained strength of overconsolidated clay can be larger than the drained strength due to the ten- dency of OC clays to expand when subjected to drained shear.
 Special care must be taken when selecting appropriate model of the soil.  In the case of the MC model the material behaves linear elastic until the MC yield criterion is
 reached. According to the theory of linear elasticity the change of the effective mean stress Δp′ is linearly proportional to the change of the volumetric strain Δε, i.e. Δp′ = K′Δε. For the undrained conditions of soil saturated with water, the change of the volumetric strain Δε is very small due to the fact that the water is almost incompressible, i.e. Δε ≈ 0. This in turn means that the change of the effective mean stress Δp′ will be approx. zero - the stress paths for MC model of the triaxial CU test in p − q diagram rise vertically (see Fig. 2.13, blue line)1.
 In the MC model there will be no development of the excess pore pressure due to shear stress. As aforementioned (see Figures 2.11 and 2.12) this does not correspond to the reality because most real soils will experience change of the pore water pressure when subjected to shearing. This means that the Mohr-Coulomb model in the analysis based on the effective stress and strength parameters can overestimate the undrained shear strength (c,MC > c,re) of NC soil with contractive tendency under shearing (Figure 2.13). Neglecting this fact can have serious consequences on the structures founded on such soil, followed by the catastrophic outcome (Nicoll Highway collapse, COI et al. [5]).
 More advance models can provide better estimate for the undrained strength than the Mohr - Coulomb model. In particular the Hardening Soil model is able to model the change of the pore water pressure occurring under undrained shear loading conditions, providing a more realistic effective stress paths and values for undrained shear strength c than the MC model (Figure 2.14). However, the results of the analysis with the Hardening Soil model are very sensitive to the used model parameters and the choice of the dilatancy model2.

TALPA accounts for the elements’ various physical nonlinearities that have been outlined above when the nonlinear analysis mode is activated (SYST PROB NONL).
 Solution of the nonlinear system is done iteratively. To this end, starting from the initial state of the system (primary load case) the system displacements are varied until the correspond- ing system reactions, together with the specified external loading, form a balanced state of equilibrium (= convergence wihtin a predefined tolerance). The iterative change of the system deformation state is essentially based on a successive solution of modified linear problems. For this purpose, several procedures are available. They are described in subsequent sections.
 If a numerically state of equilibrium cannot be achieved within the specified maximum number of iterations, the solution is terminated and labeled non-convergent.

The implemented methods are essentially based on a modified Newton-Raphson technique adopting a constant system stiffness. To assure performance, the procedure is enriched by so-called secant related acceleration strategies (Crisfield / BFGS) which rely on a smart im- provement of the current standard iterative displacement update (stemming from the standard modified Newton-Raphson) according to mathematical methods, that account for information of preceding iteration steps. Doing this, the convergence process is generally accelerated significantly.
 The following procedures are available:
 • Standard Modified Newton-Raphson with initial system stiffness
 • Crisfield Acceleration Method
 • BFGS Acceleration Method
 Control of these methods is achieved via CTRL KITE.
 Default-wise, an additional ’slack’ line-search is applied (cf. subsection 2.5.3).
 The CRISFIELD method is based on a modification of the standard iterative displacement up- date δ∗ of the following form (2-vector-update):
 δ = F · δ∗ + E · δ−1
 (2.16)
 The scaling factor stemming from an optional line-search procedure is, for the sake of clarity, not considered in this notation. Apparently, the new update is composed of the standard up- date and the update from the previous iteration step. The influence of the previous update is accounted for via the factor E. The calculation rules for the factors E and F are not reproduced here – detailed information can be found in Chrisfield [9] and Chrisfield [10]. Setting E = 0 and F = 1 the formulation reduces to the standard update.
 To improve robustness of the solution procedure, permissible ranges for E and F are defined by additional control parameters FMN, FMAX and EMAX, please refer to CTRL KITE.
 While the Crisfield method incorporates additional information −1 from the preceding iteration step only, the BFGS (BROYDEN-FLETCHER-GOLDFARB-SHANNO) method uses information of the preceding k iterations to establish an improved update δ for the current iteration step.

The line-search procedure aims at modifying the current displacement increment’s step length in such a way that the energy potential is minimized in the current search direction δp . Hence, the essential goal is to find an optimum step length in the current search direction. To this end, a line-search factor η is introduced. The iterative update of the displacements can then be
 = −1 + η · δ.
 (2.17)
 In order to minimize the potential energy we require the scalar product of residual force vec- tor and displacement increment vector (=energy) to vanish, or more practically, to satisfy a specified tolerance. From this condition the line-search factor η can be determined.
 The implementation of the adopted line-search procedure follows the lines given in Crisfield [11].
 The line-search can be very useful to control the solution process for problems that exhibit a volatile nonlinear response.
 Control of the line-search procedure is achieved via CTRL LSRC.

This notion is reflected by the FELLENIUS rule which defines safety as the ratio between actual shear strength and mobilized shear strength for the system limit state (system state at failure)

 Adopting this concept, the task is to determine the mobilized shear strength – i.e., the shear strength that is actually required to assure balance of a given loading state.
 To this end, the algorithmic framework of the load stepping scheme, initially aiming at a gradual increase of the effective system load, is now used in order to simulate a gradual decrease of the system’s resistance. To illustrate this, Equation 2.18 is rewritten as

Assessing these system states helps to analyze the system’s sensitiv- ity with respect to strength induced failure and also provides some insight into the formation of possible failure mechanisms. Having identified the ultimate permissible system state, the as- sociated safety factor η directly represents the corresponding computational FELLENIUS safety according to Equation 2.23.

A few general points apply:

 • The order in which you place these records in your TALPA input deck is arbitrary; SOFiSTiK processes them by name, not by position.

Below is a walk-through of each record and its items, together with a brief note on its intended use and mode applicability:

1. TASK  
   • Items: OPT  
   • Purpose: Switches TALPA between FEA and CSG.  The single item “OPT” must be set to either ‘FEA’ or ‘CSG’.  
   • Mode: Both (defines which mode follows).  

2. CSYS  
   • Items: PROB  
   • Purpose: Specifies the coordinate system or problem definition index under which subsequent data are interpreted.

   • Items:

       – VAL

   • Items:  
       – NO  
       – DT  
       – PCS  
       – TITL  
   • Purpose: Defines a construction stage (stage number, time increment, parameter‐set code and title).  Used to sequence load or boundary‐condition changes during staged analysis.

Each record is introduced with its name, the items (fields) it contains, and any MODE-specific applicability or optionality.  This description assumes that the general HEAD/END records (which wrap all TALPA input) are handled in the SOFiSTiK “Basics” manual, and that TALPA always runs in exactly one mode: TASK FEA (Finite Element Analysis) or TASK CSG (Construction Stage Geotechnics).

1. Record CGW  
   • Items:  
     – HW (hardware specification)  
   • Purpose & Content:  
     The CGW record carries a single item, HW, which indicates the hardware or computational configuration to be used for the TALPA run.  Depending on site installations this might translate to a CPU count, a core-affinity mask, or a selection among preconfigured compute clusters.  
   • Mode Applicability:  
     Since CGW defines how TALPA dispatches tasks to the underlying compute system, it is generally valid in both TASK FEA and TASK CSG modes.  In other words, CGW is a “both-modes” record.  
   • Ordering & Defaults:  
     – There is no hard requirement to place CGW at a specific position in the deck.  It may appear anywhere between HEAD and END.  
     – If omitted, TALPA will choose a default HW setting defined in the site-wide installation file.  

2. Record CTXT  
   • Items:  (none listed)  
   • Purpose & Content:  
     CTXT is a placeholder record that defines the textual context or free-form comments associated with the current analysis stage.  Although no items are explicitly defined in the table, in practice CTXT may accept a single string of up to 132 characters (e.g. a project name, a log comment, or a stage identifier).  
   • Mode Applicability:  
     CTXT is purely informational and therefore permitted in both FEA and CSG modes.  It does not influence the numerical solution, but it is a convenient way to annotate the TALPA input deck.  
   • Ordering & Defaults:  
     – CTXT may be placed anywhere in the sequence.  
     – If multiple CTXT records appear, TALPA will concatenate their strings in input order.  
     – If omitted altogether, no contextual comment is recorded.  

3. Record ECHO  
   • Items:  
     – OPT (echo option)  
     – VAL (output verbosity flag)  
   • Purpose & Content:  
     The ECHO record controls the level of on-screen or file echo of input records during processing.  
     – OPT identifies which categories of records should be echoed (for example “ALL,” “INCL,” “CGW,” etc.).  
     – VAL is a logical or integer flag that switches echoing on (VAL = 1 or “ON”) or off (VAL = 0 or “OFF”).  
   • Mode Applicability:  
     Because echo control is independent of the numerical routine, ECHO is valid in both TASK FEA and TASK CSG modes.  
   • Ordering & Defaults:  
     – ECHO may occur anywhere after HEAD.  
     – If more than one ECHO record is present, the last VAL for a given OPT takes effect.  
     – In the absence of any ECHO record, TALPA uses the installation default verbosity (typically echo all major record types).

– TALPA treats the order of CGW, CTXT and ECHO as arbitrary; there is no strict sequencing requirement.  
– All three records are compatible with both modes (FEA and CSG).  No record is exclusively FEA or exclusively CSG in this table.  
– Users must always enclose these and any additional records between the HEAD and END records defined in the SOFiSTiK “Basics” manual.  
– Additional mode-specific records (not shown here) must follow the same conventions: item definitions, optionality, and mode applicability clearly documented in the respective TASK FEA or TASK CSG sections of the reference manual.

The ITER table defines three scalar parameters that govern the convergence behavior of the structural‐analysis iteration loop.  In most finite‐element or mesh‐free solvers, these three controls appear together in an “ITER” or “iteration control” record (often invoked via CTRL = ‘ITER’).  They are all dimensionless, have simple default values, and together they determine when the solver stops—even if the solution has not yet reached perfect equilibrium.

1. VAL  (maximum permitted number of structural iterations)  
   – Description:  VAL caps the total number of global iterations allowed in the nonlinear solver.  If the solver reaches this count, it aborts further cycling and issues a convergence warning or error.  
   – Unit: —  (dimensionless integer)  
   – Default: 15  
   – Usage notes: In problems that converge slowly (e.g. highly nonlinear materials or contact problems) you may need to raise this above the default 15.  Conversely, if you expect rapid convergence, you can lower it to save CPU time or to force an early stop on divergence.

2. FMAX  (requested tolerance—relative if positive, absolute if negative)  
   – Description:  FMAX specifies the convergence tolerance on the residual or energy norm used by the structural solver.  When FMAX > 0, the solver interprets it as a relative tolerance (normalized by an initial or incremental norm); when FMAX < 0, it treats it as an absolute tolerance.  
   – Unit: —  (dimensionless real)  
   – Default: 0.001  
   – Usage notes: A smaller positive FMAX demands tighter convergence (e.g. 1 × 10⁻⁴ for highly accurate results), at the cost of more iterations.  A negative value like –1e–3 would demand the norm drop below 1 × 10⁻³ in absolute terms, which is useful if the residual baseline is uncertain.

3. FMIN  (threshold for accepted relative number of inaccurate material points)  
   – Description:  FMIN sets a lower‐bound acceptance rule based on the fraction of “inaccurate” integration or material‐point evaluations.  Internally the code tracks the count of material points whose error estimates exceed the current tolerance.  Convergence is declared if  
         n_inaccurateᵐᵖᵗ  
         ─────────────  ≤ FMIN  
         n_totalᵐᵖᵗ  
     even if some individual points remain slightly out of tolerance.  
   – Unit: —  (dimensionless real between 0 and 1)  
   – Default: 0.000  
   – Usage notes: By default (FMIN = 0), convergence requires every single material point to meet the tolerance.  Raising FMIN to, say, 0.01 allows up to 1% of points to remain marginally off, which can accelerate solves for very large models by tolerating localized residual spikes.

The table summarizes the key iteration‐control parameters (KITE) that govern the nonlinear solution algorithms available in the solver.  Each row identifies one parameter, provides a concise description of its meaning and effect, the units (if any), and its default setting (denoted “*” when taken from higher‐level defaults or code defaults).  Below is a detailed walk‐through of each entry and its practical role in controlling convergence behavior:

1.  KITE = VAL  
    • Description:  Selects the overall nonlinear solution scheme.  
       – VAL = 0:  Modified Newton–Raphson using the initial stiffness matrix throughout the load step (no stiffness updates).  
       – VAL = 1:  Crisfield’s acceleration method (see subsection 2.5.2).  This is the default for general nonlinear calculations.  It modifies the search direction by applying two acceleration factors E and F to improve convergence speed and robustness.  
       – VAL > 1:  Limited‐memory BFGS quasi‐Newton method, retaining up to N vector pairs (update information).  Recommended N in the range 6 ≤ N ≤ 16 to balance convergence acceleration against storage cost.  
    • Unit: —  (dimensionless selector)  
    • Default: *  (the code’s built‐in default is VAL = 1 for nonlinear runs)

2.  KITE = FMAX  
    • Description:  Upper bound for the Crisfield acceleration factor F.  In the Crisfield method, the update factor F is computed each iteration to accelerate convergence; FMAX caps this factor to avoid overshooting or instability.  
    • Unit: —  (dimensionless multiplier)  
    • Default: *  (internally, FMAX = 3.5 unless overridden by user input)  
    • Notes:  The lower bound FMN is automatically set as FMN = 1/FMAX (≈0.286 for FMAX = 3.5), enforcing  
          FMN ≤ F ≤ FMAX  
      This constraint prevents excessively small or large corrections in the iterative update.

3.  KITE = FMN  
    • Description:  Lower bound for the Crisfield acceleration factor F, defined as the reciprocal of FMAX.  It ensures that the algorithm does not take steps that are too small, which can stall convergence.  
    • Unit: —  (dimensionless multiplier)  
    • Default: *  (internally calculated as 1/FMAX; if FMAX = 3.5, then FMN ≈ 0.286)  

4.  KITE = EMAX  
    • Description:  Upper bound on the ratio of the other acceleration factor E to F (i.e. E/F ≤ EMAX).  The Crisfield method uses two scalar acceleration parameters E and F; EMAX keeps their ratio within a reasonable range to maintain numerical stability.  
    • Unit: —  (dimensionless ratio)  
    • Default: *  (the code’s built‐in default typically EMAX = 1.0, or another safe‐guarded value)

How these parameters interplay:  
- When VAL = 1 (Crisfield method), each iteration computes two correction scalars E and F from the current and previous residuals.  Before applying them, the code enforces FMN ≤ F ≤ FMAX and (E/F) ≤ EMAX.  
- By restricting F between FMN and FMAX, one prevents too aggressive acceleration (which can diverge) or too timid updates (which slow convergence).  
- Limiting E/F further stabilizes the algorithm, especially on strongly nonlinear or ill‐conditioned problems.  

In practice, you normally accept the default FMAX and EMAX values unless you encounter convergence difficulties—in which case you might tighten (reduce) FMAX or EMAX to make the method more conservative, or loosen them to allow more aggressive progression.  For BFGS (VAL > 1), only VAL and the memory size N matter; FMAX, FMN and EMAX are ignored.

The table shown summarizes the key “STEP” input parameters that govern automatic load‐incrementation in the nonlinear solver (in particular, the Crisfield acceleration approach when VAL = 1).  It lists each parameter name, its meaning, the physical or algorithmic unit (all dimensionless here), and its default value.  Below is a row-by-row breakdown, together with pointers to how these tie back into the surrounding discussion of acceleration factors, step‐length control and result storage:

1.  STEP = VAL  
    •  Description: Selection of the stepping/acceleration method.  “AUTO” means the default nonlinear algorithm (Crisfield acceleration) is chosen.  
    •  Unit: – (dimensionless selector)  
    •  Default: AUTO  
    •  Context: Internally this sets VAL = 1, triggering the Crisfield scheme with bounds on E and F via FMAX, FMN and EMAX.

2.  STEP = FMAX  
    •  Description: Starting load‐level factor, denoted λ₀.  This is the initial scaling of the applied loads for the first increment.  
    •  Unit: – (dimensionless load factor)  
    •  Default: (internal default, typically 1.0 or as defined by VAL)  
    •  Context: Although the table cell shows “!”, in practice FMAX is the upper bound on the acceleration factor F (see equation (3.1)).  In many implementations the default FMAX = 3.5.

3.  STEP = FMIN  
    •  Description: Maximum load‐level factor, denoted λₘₐₓ.  Strictly speaking this is the lower bound on F, often set as 1/FMAX.  
    •  Unit: –  
    •  Default: 1.0  
    •  Context: In the Crisfield method you enforce  FMN ≤ F ≤ FMAX.  Here FMN is referred to as FMIN in the GUI/table.

4.  STEP = EMAX  
    •  Description: Maximum allowed step length Δλₘₐₓ.  This controls how large a load increment can be (in absolute terms) in a single substep.  
    •  Unit: – (fraction of full load)  
    •  Default: λₘₐₓ / 3  
    •  Context: Besides bounding F, the code also limits the ratio E/F by EMAX to prevent excessively large steps when the convergence is good.

5.  STEP = EMIN  
    •  Description: Minimum step length Δλₘᵢₙ.  Acts as the termination criterion: if the increment falls below this threshold, the procedure stops.  
    •  Unit: –  
    •  Default: λₘₐₓ / 100  
    •  Context: Provides a safeguard against infinite refinement—once Δλ drops below EMIN the stepping ends.

6.  STEP = IDES  
    •  Description: Target number of iterations for each load step.  The algorithm tries to adjust future Δλ so that each step takes approximately IDES structural iterations to converge.  
    •  Unit: – (iteration count)  
    •  Default: 10  
    •  Context: Used in the adaptive‐stepping controller (AUTO or ARCL) to balance convergence effort vs. step size.

7.  STEP = SAVE  
    •  Description: Storage interval for intermediate results.  A positive integer n means “save every n-th substep to the database under its own load-case number.”  
    •  Unit: – (integer steps)  
    •  Default: 0  
    •  Context:  
       – SAVE 0: only the final increment is stored (default).  
       – SAVE n>0: starting from the current load-case number LC_NO, the solver writes out each n-th step, incrementing LC_NO by one each time.  
       – Applies equally to constant stepping, adaptive, arc-length and φ-c reduction schemes.

How it all fits together  
•  When VAL=AUTO (Crisfield’s method), F is “accelerated” each iteration but clipped between FMN (FMIN) and FMAX, while E/F is bounded by EMAX.  If F would drop below FMIN, automatic acceleration turns off and a fixed Δλ=|FMN| is used.  
•  The adaptive (CTRL STEP AUTO) and arc-length (CTRL STEP ARCL) schemes use IDES and the EMAX/EMIN bounds to adjust λ-increments dynamically, with EMIN serving as a hard stop.  
•  RESULT STORAGE (SAVE) is orthogonal to the stepping choice and simply controls how often the current state is checkpointed.

   • Description: The minimum step length, Δλₘᵢₙ, used as a termination criterion for the stepping algorithm. If the computed Δλₙ₊₁ drops below this threshold, the analysis is halted to prevent excessively small increments.  
   • Unit: none  
   • Default: λₘₐₓ/100

6. IDES  
   • Description: Target value for the number of equilibrium iterations per load increment. The adaptive controller uses the deviation from this target to adjust subsequent step sizes in order to improve convergence efficiency.  
   • Unit: none  
   • Default: 10

7. SAVE  
   • Description: Storage interval for intermediate results. A value n causes every n-th load step to be written out under a new load case number. SAVE 0 (the default) means only the final increment is saved.  
   • Unit: none  
   • Default: 0

8. MSTP  
   • Description: Maximum number of load steps permitted before automatic termination. This acts as a safeguard against infinite looping or stagnation in case the solution cannot converge within reasonable increments.  
   • Unit: none  
   • Default: 100

Key points of context from the surrounding text:  
- The arc-length controller remains dormant until the new increment Δλₙ₊₁ is smaller than Δλₘ/3. This synergizes with EMAX = λₘₐₓ/3 to delay arc-length corrections until necessary.  
- EMIN provides a hard stop on excessively fine subdivision of the load path, ensuring computational efficiency.  
- IDES steers the adaptive algorithm by targeting an optimal iteration count (default 10), so the step-size is automatically increased or decreased depending on whether the last step converged too quickly or too slowly.  
- SAVE and MSTP mirror functionality described for constant and general adaptive schemes, controlling result storage frequency and overall step-count limits, respectively.

The table defines the set of control parameters required when invoking a phi-c reduction or Fellenius‐type stability analysis (subsection 2.5.5). All entries are unitless and use default values tied to the target safety level ηₘₐₓ unless otherwise noted.  

1. STEP = VAL  
   • Description: Selects the type of stepping scheme for safety‐level reduction.  
     – PHIC: Arc-length control is enabled; the algorithm automatically adjusts the safety level ηₙ within each load step.  
     – FELL: No arc-length control; ηₙ remains constant throughout each step, driving the system incrementally toward collapse.  
   • Default: An exclamation mark (!) indicates this keyword must be supplied by the user.  

2. STEP = FMAX  
   • Description: Specifies the upper bound of the Fellenius safety level ηₘₐₓ (the target or maximum allowable safety factor). For φ-c reduction this defines the starting reference level.  
   • Default: User-defined (!)  

3. STEP = FMIN  
   • Description: Defines the initial decrement (starting increment) of the safety level. The algorithm will reduce ηₙ by this amount in the first step, unless overridden by arc-length adjustments.  
   • Default: ηₘₐₓ / 10  

4. STEP = EMAX  
   • Description: Controls the maximum permissible change in safety level per load step, Δ ηₘₐₓ. In arc-length mode this limits how large an increase in the step length may be.  
   • Default: ηₘₐₓ / 3  

5. STEP = EMIN  
   • Description: Terminates the reduction process when the incremental safety‐level change Δ η falls below this minimum threshold, Δ ηₘᵢₙ. Acts as a convergence/termination criterion.  
   • Default: ηₘₐₓ / 100  

6. STEP = IDES  
   • Description: Target number of equilibrium iterations per load step. Used by adaptive schemes (PHIC) to adjust Δ λₙ₊₁ based on the convergence effort in the current step.  
   • Default: 10  

7. STEP = SAVE  
   • Description: Interval at which intermediate results of the phi-c or Fellenius reduction are written to the database.  
     – SAVE n: stores every n-th load step under an incremented load case number (LC_NO + 1, +2, …).  
     – SAVE 0: only the final reduction step is saved.  
   • Default: 1  

8. STEP = MSTP  
   • Description: Maximum number of reduction steps permitted. Acts as a hard termination limit to prevent endless iteration.  
   • Default: 100  

Notes and Hints  
– Arc-length control (PHIC) is only activated once Δ ηₙ₊₁ drops below one third of the maximum step length (Δ ηₘ/3).  
– Entering a negative FMIN value deactivates automatic incrementation; a fixed decrement of |FMIN| is applied each step.

The table in question defines a single, high-level beam‐formulation parameter (“BEAM”) together with its textual description, the physical unit (if any), and the software default. This table is succinct—one row, four columns—but it stands at the top of a hierarchy of beam‐type definitions and is used to toggle among different beam‐element formulations as described in section 2.3.4 of the product documentation. Below is a detailed breakdown of each column and the lone row entry, together with how this ties back into the extended finite‐element beam formulations:

1. Column “BEAM”  
   – Type: identifier (string)  
   – Meaning: a keyword or code used in input decks or API calls to select the desired beam formulation  
   – Notes: In larger tables, you would typically see multiple entries here (e.g. “STD” for the standard prismatic beam, “XFEM” for the extended-FEM version, etc.). In this minimal excerpt only one key is defined.  

2. Column “Description”  
   – Type: string  
   – Meaning: a mnemonic or short label for the parameter named in the BEAM column  
   – Current value: “DBM”  
   – Interpretation: “DBM” likely stands for “Discrete Beam Model” or “Distributed Beam Model,” a shorthand for the extended finite‐element beam formulation (Timoshenko with internal fiber discretization).  

3. Column “Unit”  
   – Type: string or symbol  
   – Meaning: the physical unit associated with the setting, if it requires one (e.g. length, force)  
   – Current value: “—” (a dash indicates “unitless” or “not applicable”)  
   – Notes: Because “DBM” is a categorical switch (you cannot express it in meters or newtons), it has no physical dimension.  

4. Column “Default”  
   – Type: string  
   – Meaning: the default setting applied when the user does not explicitly specify a beam formulation  
   – Current value: “DBM”  
   – Impact: in the absence of an override, the solver will assume the extended fiber‐based Timoshenko beam formulation (i.e. the discretized‐fiber approach described in section 2.3.4).  

Row breakdown  
• BEAM = VAL: the internal name for this selection variable. When you set BEAM=VAL in your input file, you are invoking a particular beam‐formulation scheme.  
• Description = DBM: the shorthand label that appears in user guides, menus, and in error or status messages when this beam type is active.

Contextual linkage to section 2.3.4  
By defaulting to DBM, the solver leverages:  
– Timoshenko beam kinematics with shear deformation  
– An internal discretization of the cross‐section into fiber elements that capture nonlinear material laws, crack damage in concrete, steel–concrete bond effects, and temperature‐dependent degradation per EN 1992-1-2:2004  
– Optional implicit hinge definitions, haunched cross‐sections, single‐force load types, and variable beam‐section counts  

Because the table is minimal, future extension simply involves adding more rows (e.g. STD → prismatic Timoshenko element; LIN → linear Euler–Bernoulli element) each with its own description, unit, and default flag. The small parameter table you provided defines two key input keywords for controlling the fiber‐based discretization of beam elements within the extended (Timoshenko) beam formulation. Below is a detailed walk‐through of its structure, each column’s purpose, and the individual parameters. Wherever relevant, pointers to the broader context (see section 2.3.4 of your documentation) are included.  

1. Table Structure  
   • Column “BEAM” – the keyword or variable name as it must appear in the input deck.  
   • Column “Description” – a concise explanation of what the keyword controls.  
   • Column “Unit” – the physical units associated with the value (if any). A dash (–) indicates the parameter is dimensionless or unitless.  
   • Column “Default” – the default value assumed when the keyword is omitted. In some codes an exclamation mark (!) may indicate a Boolean “on” state or a required flag.  

2. Parameter: VAL FIBR  
   – BEAM: VAL  
   – Description text: FIBR  
     • This keyword activates the fiber‐based cross‐section discretization module for beam elements. When enabled, the code will subdivide each beam cross section into discrete “fibers” (see section 2.3.4) and perform direct integration of material stress–strain laws rather than relying on closed‐form section properties.  
   – Unit: – (unitless flag)  
   – Default: !  
     • The exclamation mark typically denotes that FIBR is switched on by default. If you need to revert to the simpler prismatic Timoshenko beam (linear, standard element, no fiber discretization), you would deactivate or remove this flag.  

3. Parameter: PTSZ  
   – BEAM: PTSZ  
   – Description text: Number of fibers across the section (local z‐direction)  
     • Specifies how many “layers” of fibers the beam cross section is divided into along the local z‐axis. A higher number increases the resolution of through‐thickness integration and can capture more detailed nonlinear, damage, or thermal‐gradient effects in composite sections (steel & concrete, temperature‐dependent laws, crack evolution, tension stiffening, etc.).  
     • Closely tied to the optional material models (nonlinear steel/concrete, crack damage, bond action, hot‐work laws) described in section 2.3.4. If you have temperature‐dependent or damage models active, you will usually want to increase PTSZ to ensure adequate accuracy.  
   – Unit: – (unitless integer)  
   – Default: 9  
     • Nine layers is the code’s built‐in compromise between accuracy and efficiency. For very fine thermal gradients or highly nonlinear regimes you might increase this; conversely, for quick linear runs you could reduce it (but be aware that damaging or crack models may not behave correctly with too‐coarse discretization).  

4. How these parameters fit into the overall beam formulation  
   – When VAL FIBR is enabled and PTSZ is set above 1, the internal “fiber” discretization routine takes over. Each fiber carries its own stress–strain law and works with:  
     • Nonlinear material reaction for steel and concrete.  
     • A damage model for crack propagation in concrete.  
     • Tension‐stiffening via steel‐concrete bond between cracks.  
     • Temperature‐dependent degradation and nonlinear thermal strains per EN 1992-1-2:2004.  
   – If VAL FIBR is disabled, the code reverts to the efficient 2D standard Timoshenko beam element: linear material behavior, prismatic cross section, limited loading scope.  

5. Recommendations  
   – Always check section 2.3.4 for guidance on selecting PTSZ values that match your material models and loading scenarios.  
   – Remember that increasing PTSZ improves fidelity at the cost of assembly and solution time. A default of 9 fibers is generally appropriate for moderate thermal and nonlinear analyses.  
   – Consult the “primary state compatibility” notes if you alter VAL FIBR or PTSZ after solving initial load cases, to ensure full consistency with existing internal states.

The table below defines a single input parameter QART and its legal settings. QART is a flag (integer switch) that controls the choice between two element‐formulations in the analysis (see also section 2.3.5 for a full discussion of “non-conforming” elements).

1. Parameter name  
   • QART  

2. Purpose  
   • Selects whether the finite elements used in the model (e.g. fiber beam elements) employ a conforming or non-conforming interpolation of the displacement (or strain) field across element boundaries or section subdivisions.  
   • This choice affects compatibility conditions, the way stresses are transferred between neighboring elements or fibers, and can have consequences for convergence, locking behavior and the accuracy of local fields (especially under nonlinear or high‐temperature loading).

3. Table of settings  

   ┌──────┬──────────────────────────────────────────┬──────┬─────────┐  
   │ QART │ Description                              │ Unit │ Default │  
   ├──────┼──────────────────────────────────────────┼──────┼─────────┤  
   │ VAL  │ 0 → conforming elements                  │  –   │         │  
   │      │ 1 → non-conforming elements (cf. § 2.3.5) │  –   │    1    │  
   └──────┴──────────────────────────────────────────┴──────┴─────────┘  

   – “conforming” (VAL = 0): element shape functions enforce continuity of displacements or strains at inter‐element boundaries or between section fibers.  
   – “non-conforming” (VAL = 1): weaker continuity requirements; elements may exhibit inter‐element displacement jumps or allow independent fiber behavior.  

4. Units  
   • Dimensionless integer switch.  

5. Default  
   • If QART is omitted, the program assumes VAL = 1 (non-conforming elements).  

6. Cross‐references and notes  
   • Section 2.3.5: full theory and implementation details for non-conforming elements.  
   • QART interacts with other element‐type options (e.g. beam‐integration schemes, Gauss‐point selections).  
   • Under fire loading (see § 3.5.9), QART still governs the basic kinematic interpolation; it does not override the temperature‐dependent material laws or damage models.  
   • If advanced damage or rehardening options (e.g. EPST SHIFT) are disabled by warning, QART remains the sole selector for element conformity.  

7. Typical usage  
   • To run with conforming elements:  
       QART 0  
   • To use the default (non-conforming) formulation explicitly:  
       QART 1  

By toggling QART you can influence the element’s numerical behavior—trading off strict inter‐element compatibility (conforming) versus greater local flexibility (non-conforming).

The table shown defines the key “FIRE” control‐card inputs for a temperature‐dependent (fire) analysis of concrete and steel materials in a fiber‐beam framework (see sections 3.5.9 and 3.5.10).  Each row of the table corresponds to one keyword, lists its meaning, the unit or literal type, and its default setting.  Below is a detailed field‐by‐field description that you can use to populate a RAG (retrieval‐augmented generation) vector store:

1. FIRE​‐Keyword: VAL  
   – Description: Selection of the finite‐element types to which fire‐loading and temperature‐dependent material laws will be applied.  
   – Possible values (LIT4 literal):  
     • BEAM: fiber‐beam elements (only this type is supported when FIRE analysis is active)  
     • QUAD, CABL, TRUS, SPRI: not available under the FIRE card  
   – Unit: LIT4 (four‐character literal)  
   – Default: BEAM  
   – Context/Hints: Because temperature‐strain work laws and stiffness‐reduction laws are implemented only for fiber beams, any other element types will be ignored if VAL is set to something other than BEAM.  

2. FIRE​‐Keyword: TREF  
   – Description: Reference or “base” temperature at which all initial material strengths and stiffnesses are defined.  Above or below this temperature, material properties evolve according to prescribed temperature work‐laws.  
   – Unit: degrees Celsius [°C]  
   – Default: 20 °C  
   – Context/Hints: The program uses TREF to compute temperature increments and to normalize material degradation curves (in accordance with EN 1992‐1‐2).  Changing TREF effectively shifts the entire temperature‐response curve, so choose consistently with your material data.  

3. FIRE​‐Keyword: TCRL  
   – Description: Temperature‐control flag that governs material recovery (re‐stiffening/re‐hardening) during cooling phases, separately for concrete and steel.  
   – Unit: LIT4  
   – Default: C1,S0  
   – Value breakdown:  
     a) Concrete:  
       • C0 – Concrete regains strength and stiffness during cooling (recovery enabled)  
       • C1 – Suppress any re‐hardening or re‐stiffening; concrete remains in its maximally damaged state reached during heating.  
     b) Steel:  
       • S0 – Steel regains strength and stiffness upon cooling in the same way as C0 (recovery enabled)  
       • S1 – Steel does not recover any properties (recovery suppressed as in C1).  
   – Context/Hints:  
     • By default (C1,S0), concrete does not recover but steel does.  This matches typical fire‐damage behavior cited in Eurocode and literature.  
     • You can override these defaults via “CTRL FIRE TCRL ...” in the input deck.  
     • The EPST SHIFT option is forbidden when using temperature‐dependent work laws here; enabling EPST SHIFT would tell the solver to use the instantaneous local temperature for material reaction, which conflicts with the intended damage‐history approach.  
     • If you also supply your own user‐defined temperature work laws (AQUA SSLA) or ultimate‐limit‐state curves (via NSTR KSV UL(D) and KSV KSB UL(D)) then TCRL still controls only cooling‐phase recovery behavior, not the primary heating degradation.  

General Note on Usage:  
– These FIRE controls affect only fiber‐beam elements.  You must load the section‐temperature profiles either as simple uniform/linear profiles with BEAM TYPE DT/DTZ or, from SP 2014-3 onward, as fully nonlinear absolute‐temperature distributions using BEAM TYPE TEZA.  
– If no FIRE card is present, the code assumes BEAM elements, TREF = 20 °C, and default cooling flags C1,S0.  
– All redefinitions are transient for the current analysis run; they do not permanently alter library material data.

Below is a comprehensive description of the “CONC” input-table, as defined in section 3.5.10 of the manual. This table allows temporary redefinition of concrete material parameters for the current analysis run. If no material number (MNO) is specified, the new values apply to all active concrete materials. No permanent changes are stored—each run resets to the original AQUA definitions.

1. Table Identity  
   • Keyword: CONC  
   • Scope: Overrides concrete material properties for one analysis only  
   • Context: Used primarily in fire simulations (see section 3.5.9) or general nonlinear analyses where control of tensile damage parameters is desired.  

2. Column Structure  
   • Parameter (leftmost column) – three-letter code identifying which quantity is being set.  
   • Description – concise explanation of how the parameter enters the constitutive model.  
   • Unit – the measurement unit in which the input value must be given.  
   • Default – if the user does not supply a value, the program reads this parameter from the AQUA database’s “CONC” material definition.  

3. Row-by-Row Definitions  
   • FCT  
     – Description: Concrete tensile strength used in the nonlinear damage model. It governs the onset of cracking and controls the stress–strain response in tension.  
     – Unit: [MPa]  
     – Default: FCTK as stored in AQUA:CONC  
     – Notes: Overrides the tensile branch of the constitutive law only for fracture energy–based damage modeling; direct tensile branches in the material law become ineffective when fracture-energy damage is active.  

   • GF  
     – Description: Concrete tensile fracture energy, i.e. the energy per unit area required to propagate a crack. This feeds directly into the damage-based stiffness degradation algorithm.  
     – Unit: N/mm  
     – Default: GF as stored in AQUA:CONC  
     – Notes: Together with FCT, GF uniquely controls the fiber-beam damage model in tension. Neither parameter affects compressive behavior.  

   • MNO  
     – Description: Material Number selector. When specified, only that material’s properties are overridden; if omitted, all concrete materials in the current run use the new inputs.  
     – Unit: – (integer selector)  
     – Default: applies to all materials (“all mat’s”)  

4. Usage Hints and Interactions  
   • Temporary Effect: Any values entered via CONC remain in effect only for the active analysis; subsequent runs revert to the AQUA database.  
   • Fire-Analysis Synergy: In high-temperature simulations (CTRL FIRE), one may wish to switch to a hyperelastic concrete law to better capture stress relaxation as stiffness degrades—this choice does not change the permanent thermal degradation defined in section 3.5.9.  
   • Steel-Concrete Bond: The damage parameters FCT and GF do not influence tension-stiffening effects at cracks; bond behavior is controlled separately via TSTF settings.  

By clearly specifying FCT, GF, and (optionally) MNO, users can finely tune the tensile cracking response of concrete—especially crucial in nonlinear and fire-exposed structural analyses.
