The input table spans two related topics—“Fire Analysis of Temperature‐Dependent Material Behavior” (section 3.5.9) and “Concrete Material Controls” (section 3.5.10)—and is organized by keyword.  Each entry in the table typically provides:

 • Keyword  
 • Applicability (e.g. concrete vs. steel, fiber‐beam elements only)  
 • Default behavior or adopted code model  
 • User‐input requirements or restrictions  
 • Hints and warnings  
 • References to examples or external standards  

Below is a detailed, structured description of each keyword in the table:

1. General Fire Analysis (3.5.9)  
   – AQUA SSLA  
     • If the user does not supply explicit temperature‐dependent strength/stiffness laws, the program automatically adopts those from EN 1992-1-2:2004.  
     • No user values needed unless overriding default code provisions.  

   – NSTR KSV UL(D) & KSV KSB UL(D)  
     • Used to select user-defined work laws for the Ultimate Limit State (ULS) at each discrete temperature.  
     • Mandatory when overriding the EN-1992 defaults; must be activated in the TALPA runs (see §3.13).  

   – EPST SHIFT  
     • Not permitted in fire analyses. Invocation will switch to evaluating material response on the current temperature rather than on historical maxima.  
     • Warning: Concrete must remain at its maximum‐damage state on cooling; steel will, by default, re‐stiffen on cooling.  

   – CTRL FIRE TCRL  
     • Alters the default treatment of cooling effects:  
       – Concrete: no re-stiffening; remains at maximum damage.  
       – Steel: regains stiffness and strength on cooling.  

   – CTRL FIRE  
     • Only effective for fiber‐beam elements. Activates fire load handling using beam‐type temperature loads.  
     • Supports:  
       – Constant or linear cross‐sectional temperature profiles via BEAM TYPE DT and DTZ.  
       – (Since SP 2014-3) Fully general, non-linear profiles via BEAM TYPE T EZA (absolute temperatures).  
     • Examples provided in the distribution:  
       – uniaxial-compression-fire.dat  
       – test-fire-temp-nonl.dat  

   – Program Assumptions (Hint)  
     • Concrete is assumed incapable of carrying tensile stress under fire; tensile‐strength reduction is not computed.  

2. Concrete Material Controls (3.5.10)  
   – CONC (Redefinition of Properties)  
     • Temporarily overrides all or specified concrete material properties for the current run only (no permanent overwrite).  

   – Hyperelastic Behavior Choice (Hint)  
     • Enabling hyperelasticity can simulate stress relaxation due to stiffness loss at high temperatures, preventing “locked‐in” high stresses from prior, lower‐temperature load.  
     • Does not affect the permanent temperature‐induced degradation modeled via work laws (see 3.5.9).  
     • Also applies to reinforcing steel if hyperelastic is chosen.  

   – Fiber‐Beam Fracture‐Energy Damage Model (Hint)  
     • Only the fracture energy and tensile strength parameters control damage. Any tensile branch in the concrete law is ignored.  

   – TSTF (Steel–Concrete Bond / Tension Stiffening)  
     • Automatically modifies the steel strain to reflect bond interaction as cracking evolves. Three cracking phases are recognized:  
       1. Uncracked (state I)  
       2. Crack formation  
       3. Stabilized cracking (state II)  
     • Based on CEB procedures (Comité Euro-International du Béton, §§ 3.2.3 & 7.4.3).  
     • Example illustrating tension‐stiffening effect: uniaxial-tension.dat  

   – Scope of Redefinition (Hint reiterated)  
     • If no material number is specified, all active concrete materials in the current analysis inherit the temporary override.  

Note: “Table continued on next page” indicates further entries beyond §3.5.10, but the above covers all keywords and controls defined in these two subsections.

The table shown is the CONC‐block input for defining or temporarily overriding concrete material behavior in a fibre‐beam fire or structural analysis. It consists of four columns—Keyword, Description, Unit and Default—and in the excerpt only one keyword (MTYP) is illustrated. Below is a detailed breakdown:

1. Block Name (CONC)  
   - This header identifies that all following entries relate to concrete material controls.  
   - Any redefinition under this block is temporary and applies only to the current analysis run. It does not overwrite the stored material definition in the database.  
   - If no specific material number is supplied, the input affects all active concrete materials.

2. Column “Keyword”  
   - MTYP: The only keyword shown in the excerpt. It selects the constitutive “Material type” for concrete in the analysis.

3. Column “Description”  
   - Material type  
     • PLAS: “Plastic” or elastoplastic work law. It combines an inelastic stress‐based flow rule with linear unloading and reloading. This is the default constitutive model for concrete in most fire and structural analyses.  
     • HYPE: “Hyperelastic” behavior. Under this option, the material exhibits purely reversible (elastic) deformation according to the primary loading curve; no inelastic (plastic) strains are accumulated. Unloading always follows the original work law path.  
   - Contextual hints provided elsewhere in the manual suggest that HYPE may be advantageous in fire scenarios to emulate stress relaxation arising from stiffness loss at elevated temperatures. It prevents “locked‐in” high constraint stresses that would otherwise remain if the material stiffness suddenly drops under heat.

4. Column “Unit”  
   - A dash (–) indicates that MTYP is dimensionless; it is a textual switch rather than a numeric parameter.

5. Column “Default”  
   - PLAS: Unless the user explicitly requests HYPE, the material is treated as elastoplastic by default.

6. Related Controls and Notes (from surrounding text)  
   - Fire analysis (Section 3.5.9) uses temperature‐dependent work laws and thermal strains, following EN 1992-1-2:2004 if the user does not provide custom curves.  
   - An explicit user‐defined set of work laws tied to ultimate limit‐state (via NSTR KSV UL(D), KSV KSB UL(D)) must be selected if deviating from default.  
   - EPST SHIFT (evaluating material response at actual temperature) is prohibited in this context. Instead, concrete remains in the damaged state reached on heating; steel re‐gains strength upon cooling (or can be switched via CTRL FIRE TCRL).  
   - The CONC block also interacts with fracture‐energy damage parameters in fibre beams: the fracture energy and tensile strength alone govern crack propagation, and any explicit tensile branch in the material law is ignored.  
   - Steel-concrete bond in tension (TSTF) is managed by automatic modification of steel strain through uncracked, crack formation, and stabilized cracking phases (see CEB guidelines referenced).

In practical terms, the MTYP entry under CONC lets the analyst quickly toggle between a standard, load‐dependent elastoplastic model (PLAS) and a purely elastic (HYPE) representation—especially useful when modelling stiffness degradation and stress relaxation in fire or high‐temperature loading scenarios.

The table shown defines the keyword block TSTF, which governs the tension-stiffening or steel-concrete bond behavior in a fiber‐beam fire or structural analysis. When TSTF is invoked, it temporarily overrides any default bond provisions for the current run only; no permanent material data are altered. If the user does not specify a particular material number (MNO), the settings apply to all active concrete materials in that run.

1. Parameter VAL  
   • Description: Switches the automatic bond‐modification algorithm on or off.  
     – AUTO: The program adjusts the steel strain in cracked concrete sections to model the bond-stiffening effect according to the current crack state. This simulates three cracking phases:  
        • state I – uncracked, full bond  
        • crack formation phase  
        • state II – stabilized cracking  
     – OFF: No bond modification; the steel strain remains as in an uncracked, “bare” steel element.  
   • Unit: LIT4 (a four‐character literal token)  
   • Default: AUTO  

2. Parameter FCT  
   • Description: The effective tensile strength of the concrete used in the nonlinear material reaction under bond control. This value enters the tension-stiffening formulation to scale how much tensile capacity the cracked concrete retains and thus how strongly it “pulls” on the reinforcing steel.  
   • Unit: MPa  
   • Default: FCT as defined in the concrete material block (AQUA CONC), i.e. the user’s specified or code‐default concrete tensile strength at ambient temperature.  

3. Parameter MNO  
   • Description: Material selector number. If you wish to apply TSTF settings only to a subset of your defined concrete materials, you list their material numbers here. Omit MNO to have the bond control apply to all concrete materials in the current model.  
   • Unit: — (unitless index)  
   • Default: All mat’s (every concrete material active in the run)  

Contextual notes:  
• The tension-stiffening law adapts the steel strain by reducing it in proportion to the crack opening and concrete tensile capacity, as detailed in CEB‐FIP literature.  
• This feature is especially important for capturing post‐cracking stiffness in reinforced members under fire or mechanical loads.  
• If the user chooses hyperelastic concrete behavior (section 3.5.10 hint), it may help avoid unrealistically high residual stresses due to stiffness reduction at elevated temperatures, but it does not alter the TSTF bond formulation.  
• Any redefinition via TSTF is ephemeral: once the analysis run ends, the original material data remain intact for subsequent runs.

3.5.9 FIRE Analysis of temperature dependent material behavior/ material degrada- tion for concrete and steel materials
 In a general way, the temperature dependent mechanical strength and stiffness evolution can be described by means of a family of work laws and dedicated temperature strains - i.e., one
 work law for each defined temperature level. If no corresponding explicit user input is provided (AQUA SSLA), the program adopts work laws and temperature strains according to EN 1992- 1-2:2004.
 Hint
 In the case that a user-defined set of temperature dependent work laws shall be adopted – the work laws are defined as being associated with the ultimate limit state – a cor- responding selection via NSTR KSV UL(D) and KSV KSB UL(D), respectively, in the corresponding TALPA runs is mandatory (cf. section 3.13).
 Warning
 The option EPST SHIFT is not allowed in this context.
 Activating the option triggers evaluation of the material reaction based on the actual temper- ature level of the material point under consideration. By default, concrete materials are sup- posed to not exhibit re-hardening and re-stiffening effects due to cooling; they remain in the damaged state corresponding to the maximum reached temperature in loading history. Steel materials, on the contrary, are assumed to regain stiffness and strength during cooling. Nu- merical evalulation is therefore based on the current temperature level (default setting). The default settings regarding the cooling behavior can be changed via CTRL FIRE TCRL.
 The option CTRL FIRE is effective for the fiber beam element, only. Provision of a tem- perature profile is possible with constant and linear variation over the cross-section depth; achieved simply by specifying corresponding standard beam temperature loads (BEAM TYPE DT, BEAM TYPE DTZ), i.e. temperature increments. As of SP 2014-3, additionally, the input and processing of general nonlinear temperature profiles is supported (absolute temperatures via BEAM TYPE T EZA). The simulation examples uniaxial-compression-fire.dat and test-fire- temp-nonl.dat illustrate the mechanical behavior of concrete at high temperatures.

content:
The table under consideration defines the five user-modifiable control parameters that can be passed into the SOFiSTiK nonlinear material‐law interface routine NMAT3D_USD(). In the context of nonlinear constitutive modeling, a rate‐form material law requires incremental integration of stress–strain behavior. For standard SOFiSTiK materials these integration algorithm parameters (often governing step‐size control, convergence tolerances or selective substepping) are fixed internally. However, user‐defined constitutive models can override up to five such parameters via the array Ctrl, with each element Ctrl(1) through Ctrl(5) corresponding to one of the table entries below.

Fields of the table:
 • MSTE  
   – This is the input keyword or variable tag that the user supplies in the material definition block. It tells the solver which control parameter is being specified.  
 • Description  
   – Maps the MSTE tag to the corresponding index in the Ctrl array passed to the NMAT3D_USD() subroutine. “1st parameter → Ctrl(1)” means that whenever MSTE = VAL is read, its numeric value is stored into Ctrl(1), and similarly for subsequent entries.  
 • Unit  
   – No specific physical units are assigned here (“–”). These control parameters are algorithm‐internal scalars (for example, tolerances or diffusivity factors) and do not carry direct dimensional meaning.  
 • Default  
   – The value assumed if the user does not explicitly override the parameter. Each of the five entries defaults to 0.0.

Row-by-row breakdown:
 1. VAL  
    – Represents the first control parameter (Ctrl(1)). Default = 0.0. A user may input MSTE = VAL followed by a real number to set this primary algorithmic control (for example, a primary Newton‐Raphson tolerance or a principal step‐size fraction).  
 2. FMAX  
    – The second control parameter, mapped to Ctrl(2). Default = 0.0. Often used to cap maximum allowable increments in the iterative integration or to set an upper bound on certain rate‐form quantities.  
 3. FMIN  
    – The third control parameter, corresponding to Ctrl(3). Default = 0.0. Could be used to establish a lower bound or safeguard against excessively small increments that may stall convergence.  
 4. EMAX  
    – The fourth control parameter (Ctrl(4)). Default = 0.0. May control maximum error tolerances, adaptive substepping limits or other user‐tunable aspects of the implicit integration algorithm.  
 5. EMIN  
    – The fifth and final control parameter, stored in Ctrl(5). Default = 0.0. Often serves as a lower‐threshold tolerance preventing the solver from reducing step sizes below a practical limit.

Usage notes:
 • Users define these parameters in the input deck under the section for NMAT3D_USD materials.  
 • Unspecified entries automatically assume the table’s default of 0.0.  
 • These parameters interact with internal solver logic—changing them without a clear understanding of the underlying integration scheme may lead to convergence issues or degraded performance.  
 • Because the Unit column is blank, the meaning of each parameter must be clarified by consulting the user‐defined material model documentation or source code.

Most nonlinear material laws (cf.AQUA: NMAT) are formulated in rate form. With a given total strain increment the corresponding stress increment therefore is generally established via in- tegration of the nonlinear strain rates. For this procedure powerful and robust algorithms are used – mostly implicit algorithms (Backward-Euler), in some cases explicit ones (Runge-Kutta, Forward-Euler).
 For the SOFiSTiK standard materials, control parameters of these algorithms are internally preset and not subject to user input.
 For user defined material models (cf.AQUA: NMAT), up to 5 control parameters can be modified by user input. The corresponding input is passed via the interface routine NMAT3D_USD() by means of the array Ctrl.

Prior to storage in the database, the computed displacements of the current load step are scaled by means of the factor provided here. This option is useful in the context of an in-situ stress state computation by means of the K-procedure (gravity loading), which is a common means for geomechanical analyses. In other situations, use of this option is discouraged. The system deformation computed by the K-procedure is of no practical relevance, it is a numerical
 result of generating the desired stress state, only. Specification of CTRL DEFO 0.0 effectively sets the nodal displacements to zero. The option CTRL DEFO ’AUTO’ triggers an automatic decision making procedure. In this case, the nodal displacements are set to zero, if all three subsequent conditions are fulfilled for the respective load step:
 no primary load case is referenced
 the K-procedure is used
 equilibrium (convergence) is achieved

The table under discussion defines the possible settings for the “LSEQ … VAL” parameter in TALPA’s control specification.  In the context of automatic load or time incrementation (CTRL STEP AUTO…), TALPA records every intermediate increment as a separate load case.  Because neither the total number of increments nor the final load‐case number is known ahead of time, TALPA introduces the notion of a “load case sequence.”  By assigning a sequence number rather than a fixed case number, you can reliably refer to “the last actual load case” of that sequence when building subsequent analysis steps (for example, in construction stages).  Control bits are used to turn on or off each mode; entering “CTRL LSEQ VAL 3” (binary 11) effectively activates both of the nonzero options at once.  

Structure of the table:  
- Column 1 (“LSEQ”): Always shows “VAL,” indicating that these are the legal values for the LSEQ … VAL sub-command.  
- Column 2 (“Description”): Enumerates each integer or bit-flag setting and explains its behavioral effect.  
- Column 3 (“Unit”): Shows “—,” since this parameter is dimensionless (it simply toggles behavior).  
- Column 4 (“Default”): Lists “0,” the factory default, meaning that no load‐case sequencing is active unless you explicitly change it.  

Detailed breakdown of the “Description” column entries:  
1. Value “0”  
   – Interpretation: No load case sequences are active.  
   – Effect: All primary stress states or load‐case references you enter will be treated as absolute case numbers, as in a standard non‐incremental analysis.  

2. Value “+1”  
   – Interpretation: The specification of a TALPA primary stress state is treated as a load‐case sequence (bit 1 set).  
   – Effect: Whenever you reference a primary stress state by its load‐case number, TALPA interprets that number as “I want the last (most recent) load case in the sequence.”  In other words, you don’t need to know how many increments were generated—you just say “1” (or whatever sequence index you assigned) and TALPA finds the final increment.  

3. Value “+2”  
   – Interpretation: The load case number you enter is itself a “sequence number” (bit 2 set).  
   – Effect: Rather than manually tracking which names or IDs belong to which increment, you reserve a slot in the case numbering for the entire sequence.  TALPA automatically assigns consecutive case numbers to each increment under that sequence umbrella, based on whatever the last used number was.  This guarantees continuous numbering across multiple steps without collisions.  

Using both bits simultaneously (entering “VAL 3,” since 1 + 2 = 3) enables both behaviors at once: sequence‐based referencing of existing states (+1) and automatic assignment of new sequence numbers (+2).  

Default behavior (VAL = 0) leaves TALPA in its simplest mode: no special sequence handling.  You must manually specify and track every individual load case if you do not turn on at least one of the sequence bits.

For calculations with automatic load or time incrementation (CTRL STEP AUTO...), results of the intermediate steps are normally stored in the data base, as well - as separate load cases with consecutive load case numbers. As a result of the automatic incrementation, the required number of increments is not known a priori - the same holds for the number of the load case representing the final increment. To enable referencing of this load case as primary load case for a subsequent calculation step (construction stage), TALPA uses the concept of load case sequences. Control specification is done according to bit scheme. To enable both options, CTRL LSEQ VAL 3 must be entered.

The table defines the AFIX parameter named “VAL,” which governs how the solver treats kinematic degrees of freedom (DOF) that are technically undefined—such as the rotation of a node in a purely axial (truss) element. In practice, these undefined DOF are given a very small artificial stiffness so that if any loads are applied in those directions, the resulting displacements become extremely large unless properly constrained. The AFIX:VAL setting lets you choose whether such unintentional motions trigger errors or warnings, whether they halt or let the run continue, and whether the code automatically fixes them by imposing a zero‐displacement support. Below is a breakdown of each legal integer value (0 through 7), its effect, and the overall default:

1. VAL = 0  
   - Behavior: Any degree of freedom that is exactly free (no stiffness) causes an immediate error.  
   - Outcome: The solver stops and reports an “exactly movable” DOF.  
   - Use Case: Strictest setting for catching true modeling mistakes where a DOF is left completely unconstrained.

2. VAL = 1  
   - Behavior: Any degree of freedom that moves within the numerical precision of the solver triggers an error.  
   - Outcome: The run halts and reports “movable within precision” errors.  
   - Note: Although historically called the default in some documentation, the table’s default is now VAL = 2.

3. VAL = 2  
   - Behavior: Exactly free DOF are not treated as fatal.  
   - Outcome: The solver issues a warning about each exactly movable DOF but continues execution.  
   - Default: According to the table’s “Default” column, VAL = 2 is used unless overridden.

4. VAL = 3  
   - Behavior: DOF that move only within the calculation’s precision are suppressed (i.e., treated as constrained) with a warning.  
   - Outcome: The run continues after warning messages about near‐zero stiffness DOF.

5. VAL = 4  
   - Behavior: Same as VAL = 0 in terms of error/warning logic, but with one addition: any recognizable undefined DOF is automatically provided with a fixed support (zero displacement).  
   - Outcome: Stops on “exactly movable” DOF errors, but undefined DOF are silently clamped before solving.

6. VAL = 5  
   - Behavior: Mirrors VAL = 1 (error on precision‐level DOF), while still automatically fixing any undefined DOF.  
   - Outcome: Errors out if a DOF is only “movable within precision,” but inserts fixed supports on undefined DOF.

7. VAL = 6  
   - Behavior: Aligns with VAL = 2 (warning and continue for exactly free DOF) plus automatic fixing of undefined DOF.  
   - Outcome: Warnings for true free DOF; solver continues after clamping undefined DOF in advance.

8. VAL = 7  
   - Behavior: Matches VAL = 3 (warnings for precision‐level DOF) and also imposes fixed supports on any detected undefined DOF.  
   - Outcome: Runs to completion after issuing warnings and applying zero‐displacement constraints on those marginally supported DOF.

Unit Column: not applicable (no physical unit).  
Default Setting: VAL = 2, meaning that exactly free DOF generate warnings but do not halt the analysis. This balances error checking with solver robustness, allowing runs to complete while still alerting the user to potential unconstrained motions.

AFIX controls the handling of the kinematic degrees of freedom. Recognizable undefined degrees of freedom (e.g. node rotations of a truss) are assigned a priori a small stiffness. Loads corresponding to such degrees of freedom cause very large displacements.

The table defines the single SOFiSTiK input parameter block “SOLV/VAL”, which controls the choice of linear equation solver for a finite‐element analysis.  It is structured into four columns—Parameter (SOLV → VAL), Description, Unit and Default—and summarizes the four solver options currently supported.

1. Parameter Block and Columns  
   • SOLV: the keyword identifying the solver control block.  
   • VAL: the actual integer code that selects one of the solvers.  
   • Description: a brief name for each solver corresponding to its numerical code.  
   • Unit: not applicable (marked “–”) since the parameter is dimensionless.  
   • Default: the code used if no explicit VAL is provided (Default = 3).

2. Solver Options (VAL = 0…4)  
   • VAL = 0  
     – Suppresses the solution phase entirely.  
     – Useful for creating and inspecting system loads without performing a solve.  
   • VAL = 1: Direct Skyline Solver (Gauss / Cholesky)  
     – The classical FE direct method, storing the entire skyline band of the stiffness matrix.  
     – Requires a skyline‐oriented numbering of equations.  You must invoke (CTRL OPTI 1) or (CTRL OPTI 2) during model generation to minimize bandwidth and storage.  
     – No additional VAL-parameters.  
   • VAL = 2: Iterative Sparse Solver (Conjugate Gradients)  
     – Reduces memory footprint and may offer time‐savings for large, volume‐dominated models.  
     – Supports three preconditioning variants selectable via V4:  
       · V4 = 0: Diagonal scaling (fastest, minimal memory, but many iterations).  
       · V4 = 1: Incomplete Cholesky (partial factorization, trades fill‐in vs. compute time).  
       · V4 = 2: Incomplete inverse (inferior except for dense matrices; recommended density threshold V5 ≥ 0.01).  
     – Further thresholds: V5 (relative fill‐in tolerance) and V6 (maximum bandwidth for preconditioning).  
     – Default numerical tolerance (V3) should not be changed lightly—accuracy depends on this setting.  
     – Can run in parallel under the “HISOLV” license (CTRL CORE).  
   • VAL = 3: Direct Sparse LDL Solver  
     – A modern, single‐threaded sparse LDL^T factorization (based on the Davis algorithm).  
     – Mesh generators default to an equation numbering optimized to minimize fill‐in.  
     – No extra parameters are required.  
     – Default choice (SOLV = 3) for most static analyses with multiple right‐hand sides.  
   • VAL = 4: Direct Parallel Sparse Solver (PARDISO)  
     – Leverages Intel MKL’s PARDISO library for highly optimized parallel factorization.  
     – Does not require pre‐numbering of equations—(CTRL OPTI 0) can be used to save memory in generation.  
     – Cannot reuse the factorized matrix in external programs (e.g., ELLA).  
     – Also requires “HISOLV” for multithreading (configured via CTRL CORE).

3. Default Behavior  
   – If no (CTRL SOLV) block is specified, the program uses VAL = 3 (Direct Sparse LDL Solver).  
   – Users should match the solver to problem size, memory constraints, right‐hand‐side count, and licensing.  

This concise table allows quick selection of the solver type, while the accompanying text (see CTRL OPTI and CTRL CORE sections) provides detailed guidance on numbering, preconditioning, parallelization and parameter tuning for each solver class.

The table provides a concise specification of the control parameters (CTRL SOLV 2) for invoking and steering the Iterative Equation Solver in SOFiSTiK. This solver implements a preconditioned Conjugate Gradient algorithm and is selected by setting the main solver code to VAL 2. Below is a breakdown of each column and row, together with the relevant contextual notes drawn from the broader SOFiSTiK documentation:

1. Column headings  
   • SOLV: The keyword or sub-parameter identifier used in the CTRL SOLV input line.  
   • Description: What the parameter controls.  
   • Unit: Physical unit (all entries here are dimensionless “—”).  
   • Default: The built-in default value if the user omits this option. An asterisk (*) indicates that SOFiSTiK assigns a sensible default internally; an exclamation mark (!) signals that no additional parameters are required or that the setting is mandatory for proper numbering.

2. Row summaries  
   • VAL 2 (Iterative equation solver)  
     – Description: Switches the solution strategy to the Iterative Conjugate Gradient solver.  
     – Unit: none.  
     – Default: “!” means that once you choose VAL 2, you must at least consider its sub-options; no further defaults apply as a single line.

   • V2 (Maximum number of iterations)  
     – Sets an upper bound on how many CG iterations are allowed.  
     – Default: “*” (SOFiSTiK’s internal default; typically sufficiently large for most problems, but user testing may be required).

   • V3 (Tolerance in numeric digits)  
     – Convergence criterion expressed as the number of correct digits (recommended between 5 and 15).  
     – Default: “*” (the built-in tolerance is chosen for a good trade-off between accuracy and runtime; change only after careful validation).

   • V4 (Type of preconditioning)  
     – Selects one of three preconditioning schemes that accelerate convergence by approximately factoring the stiffness matrix.  
       • 0: Diagonal Scaling – fastest, least memory, but requires many iterations; not generally recommended.  
       • 1: Incomplete Cholesky – partial factorization ignoring fill-in; good balance of convergence rate and setup cost.  
       • 2: Incomplete Inverse – forms a sparse approximate inverse; better for denser systems but generally slower than Cholesky.  
     – Default: 1 (Incomplete Cholesky).

   • V5 (Threshold value of preconditioning)  
     – A relative cutoff (0 < V5 < 1) to drop small fill-in entries during factorization, reducing memory at the possible expense of slower convergence.  
     – Default: “*” (automatic threshold; adjust via testing).

   • V6 (Maximum bandwidth in preconditioning)  
     – An integer that caps the half-bandwidth of the triangular factors in the preconditioner. A lower number saves memory but may degrade preconditioner quality.  
     – Default: “*” (SOFiSTiK chooses a bandwidth based on the overall matrix profile).

3. Contextual notes (from the broader manual)  
   • The iterative solver’s efficiency and memory footprint make it attractive for very large volume or solid-element dominated models.  
   • Correctness hinges on choosing an appropriate tolerance (V3) – changing it without re-validating results is discouraged.  
   • Preconditioning parameters (V4–V6) have a strong influence on both memory use and convergence speed; finding optimal settings often requires a few trial runs on representative load cases.

 In order to minimize computational effort, the solvers need an optimized sequence of equation numbers. This optimization step is usually performed during system generation. The programs SOFIMSHA/C by default always create a sequence which is suitable for the direct sparse solver (3). The solvers (1) or (2) however require a skyline oriented numbering which may be obtained using the option (CTRL OPTI 1) or (CTRL OPTI 2) during system generation. The table shown is a concise definition of one of SOFiSTiK’s “CTRL CORE” input parameters used to govern parallel execution in equation solvers. It belongs to the broader group of parallel-computing controls and is intended to be read in conjunction with the contextual rules and hints provided in SOFiSTiK’s documentation. Below is a detailed breakdown of every element in the table and how it ties back to the parallel-computing framework:

1. Table Structure  
   • Column 1: “CORE” – This is the keyword or parameter name that will be used in the SOFiSTiK input deck. In this particular table, the only entry under CORE is “VAL.”  
   • Column 2: “Description” – A brief, human-readable explanation of what the parameter does. For “VAL,” it indicates the number of threads to be used for parallel processing.  
   • Column 3: “Unit” – Denotes the measurement unit or data type expected for the parameter. Here it is shown as a dash (“—”), implying that “VAL” is a pure integer count without any physical unit.  
   • Column 4: “Default” – Specifies the default value assumed by the software if the user does not supply an explicit value. In this case, the default is indicated by an asterisk (“*”), which internally triggers the software’s automatic thread-count determination logic.

2. Single–Row Content  
   • CORE = VAL  
     – This is the only sub-keyword listed in this mini-table. It represents the core quantity for thread control.  
   • Description = Number of used threads  
     – Tells the user that setting VAL will directly determine how many parallel threads SOFiSTiK will spin up for eligible tasks. It does not, by itself, force parallel execution; it merely sets the ceiling.  
   • Unit = —  
     – Emphasizes that “VAL” is dimensionless. The user specifies a whole-number thread count (e.g., 4, 8, 16).  
   • Default = *  
     – The asterisk follows the hint in the preceding documentation: when VAL = * (or if no VAL is supplied), SOFiSTiK queries the operating system for the number of available physical CPU cores and uses that as the thread count. Users may override this via environment variable SOF_NUM_THREADS or by explicitly giving a numeric value to VAL.

3. How This Fits Into Parallel-Computing Logic  
   • Parallel activation is automatic for supported solvers, provided:  
     – The hardware (multi-core CPU) and OS allow threading.  
     – A valid HISOLV license is present.  
   • Override hierarchy (increasing priority):  
     a) System query → default thread count (if VAL = *).  
     b) Environment variable SOF_NUM_THREADS or “sofistik.def” parameter.  
     c) Explicit “CTRL CORE VAL” statement in the input deck.  
   • Setting VAL to 1 (or 0, depending on context) suppresses parallelism, even if the solver would otherwise run in multiple threads.

4. Usage Example  
   If you want to force SOFiSTiK to run with exactly eight threads for the next solver run, you might include in your control deck:  
     CTRL CORE 8  
   If you prefer the software to adapt to the number of physical cores, omit VAL or set it to “*”:  
     CTRL CORE *  

In summary, this little table provides the syntax and default behavior for the “VAL” argument of the “CTRL CORE” command, which is SOFiSTiK’s primary knob for controlling how many simultaneous threads are employed during permitted parallel computations. It must be used in the context of the broader rules regarding license requirements, solver support, and environment-variable overrides.

The table summarizes the three input parameters (Item) that the PHRS record accepts, together with a concise description of each parameter’s role (Description), its measurement unit (Unit), and its default setting (Default). These parameters allow the user to define a phreatic (seepage) surface in a finite‐element groundwater or soil‐structure interaction model, either as a simple horizontal plane or as a more complex shape derived from a previously computed hydraulic potential field. All three parameters are optional (no default values are assigned), but at least one of the two methods (HW or the LC+T combination) must be specified for PHRS to compute buoyant or submerged weights correctly.

1. Column: Item  
   • HW – Horizontal phreatic level  
   • LC – Reference hydraulic load-case number  
   • T  – Reference time for potential distribution  

2. Column: Description  
   • HW: “Ordinate of phreatic level.” This is the elevation (ordinate on the gravity axis) of a flat, horizontal phreatic surface. If only HW is provided, the program assumes a uniform groundwater level everywhere. Under this condition, finite elements situated below that elevation use the specified “specific weight under buoyancy,” while those above it use “specific weight” (per MAT or MATE definitions in the AQUA manual).  
   • LC: “Reference number of hydraulic load case with potential heights.” When LC is specified (in combination with T), the program retrieves a previously computed hydraulic-potential distribution from the load case identified by LC.  
   • T: “Reference time of potential distribution.” In conjunction with LC, this parameter tells the program which time step (or loading stage) of the selected hydraulic analysis to use when locating the actual phreatic surface as an equipotential contour.  

3. Column: Unit  
   • HW is measured in meters [m].  
   • LC is an integer index (dimensionless) that refers to a particular hydraulic load case.  
   • T is measured in seconds [sec].  

4. Column: Default  
   • All three items have a default of “–,” indicating that they are optional by default but must be provided in one of the two valid combinations:  
      – Specify HW alone to define a flat phreatic surface.  
      – Specify LC and T together to define a curvilinear phreatic surface from an existing hydraulic‐potential result.  

Contextual notes:  
– In the AQUA modeling framework, PHRS connects to the buoyancy calculation. Once the phreatic surface is known, AQUA automatically applies buoyant or non-buoyant weights to each finite element based on its centroid’s position relative to the phreatic surface.  
– The HW approach replicates the classic “constant‐head” boundary; the LC+T approach enables modeling transient or spatially variable groundwater levels (for example, in a dewatering scenario or when seepage paths are nonuniform).  
– If both HW and LC+T are provided, most implementations will typically prioritize the LC+T option for greater fidelity, though this behavior should be verified against the specific solver’s manual.

PHRS
 Record PHRS facilitates a phreatic surface definition. According to their relative position re- garding the specified phreatic level, the finite elements’ self-weight is then automatically com- puted using either the "specific weight" or the "specific weight under buoyancy" (see AQUA manual, command MAT/ MATE).
 HW defines a horizontal phreatic surface by specification of the corresponding ordinate on the gravity axis (analogous to HW option in record GRP).
 Alternatively, via load case number LC and time T a hydraulic potential distribution may be referenced, from which the program automatically computes position of the phreatic surface. Using this option, curved phreatic surface shapes - which may arise, e.g., as a result from a local ground water lowering - can be treated in a convenient and consistent manner.

The table defines the input fields for the PLC record, which selects and configures a “primary load case” in the finite-element analysis. Each row corresponds to one keyword (Item) you may specify; the columns give its meaning, required unit (if any), and the default value assumed when you omit it.

1. Column headings  
   • Item: the field name used in the PLC record  
   • Description: what the field controls or represents  
   • Unit: the type of value to supply (“–” means a plain number, “LIT” means a literal token)  
   • Default: the value assumed if you do not explicitly supply one

2. Rows / Items

  • LC  
    – Description: Load case number. This is the numerical identifier under which the selected primary stress/displacement state will be stored or applied.  
    – Unit: –  
    – Default: !  (an exclamation mark indicates that no default exists—you must supply it.)

  • TYPE  
    – Description: Specifies how the primary load case is to be treated. Three literal options are available:  
      · ACTI: “Activated loads.”  Total loads are used and stresses from the referenced load case are activated as external loading.  No additional displacements are introduced.  
      · FULL: “Full superposition.”  Displacements from the primary load case are added on top of those already active in the current step.  Use this when you wish to combine load‐case deflections with existing ones.  
      · S2L: “Stress‐to‐load transformation.”  Converts an existing stress state into the equivalent nodal load vector.  Useful when you have a stress field (e.g. from eigenmode or analytical prestress) but lack the original loads.  
    – Unit: LIT (you must type one of the three tokens)  
    – Default: ACTI  

  • LADD  
    – Description: Additive load case number. If specified, this secondary case (often an eigenstress or eigenmode shape) is superimposed on the primary state.  
    – Unit: –  
    – Default: –  (a dash means “no additive case”)

  • FADD  
    – Description: Factor for the additive load case (LADD). The loads/displacements from LADD are multiplied by FADD before being summed.  
    – Unit: –  
    – Default: 1.0  

  • FS2L  
    – Description: Scaling factor used only when TYPE=S2L. After generating the nodal load vector from stresses, it is multiplied by FS2L. A value of –1.0 (the default) produces a load vector identical to the one that originally created the stress state.  
    – Unit: –  
    – Default: –1.0  

Additional context:  
• Entering PLC in the SYST record (system startup) is equivalent to TYPE=FULL by default.  
• If you combine PLC with the GRP record (group‐wise load control), pay special attention to GRP defaults (FACL, FACD) and to how PLC’s TYPE setting interacts with group factors.  
• In S2L mode the program only builds and stores the load vector; it does not solve the FE system. Under S2L, GRP factors default to FACL=1.0 and FACD=0.0.

 PLC
 The record PLC selects a primary stress state that defaults for all element groups that are active in the current anaylsis step. Default settings may still be changed via the GRP command. Entering PLC in record SYST is equivalent to specifying TYPE FULL. Displacements of the primary load case are added to the ones of the currently active load case if and only if PLC has TYPE FULL or PLC has been provided in the record SYST.
 Further you may select with LADD an additional load case, which contains eigenstresses or eigen mode shapes, to be added to the primary state with a factor. Stresses above the yield limit will then be reduced with a non-linear analysis. As there are no equivalent external load patterns available in general, a calculation as activated primary load case is only reasonable in special cases.
 The option S2L generates a nodal load configuration from a corresponding stress state. This is useful particularly for the case of given system stress states where a corresponding constituting loading state is missing (e.g. analytical primary stress state, stress state from eigenmode analysis). This constituting loading state might e.g. be required for a nonlinear analysis with total loads. Calculation of the load vector is essentially analogous to the assembly of the global system of equations’ load vector ("right hand side"). Thus, the resulting load vector originates from the summation of "inner" loads from the primary stress state as stated in the GRP control (FACL) and all referenced "external" loads. The so obtained nodal load vector finally is scaled with the factor FS2L and stored under the current load case number. Any other loads that are possibly stored under the current load case number are deleted by this procedure! The actual solution of the FE system is omitted in the S2L mode, the program terminates after the load generation process. In S2L mode, GRP control factors FACL and FACD default to 1.0 and 0.0, respectively. Along with FS2L=-1.0, for this case a nodal load configuration is generated that exactly resembles the generating one of the referenced primary load case.

In S2L mode, GRP control factors FACL and FACD default to 1.0 and 0.0, respectively. Along with FS2L=-1.0, for this case a nodal load configuration is generated that exactly resembles the generating one of the referenced primary load case..
 The simultaneous use of the record PLC and the group control via the record GRP requires special attention regarding default settings.

Below is a field-by-field breakdown of the TPLC “input table” and how each entry is used when pulling temperature distributions from HYDRA.  This description is intended to be stored alongside your other RAG-indexed metadata (see also CTRL, GRP, LC, PLC).

1.  LC1  
    • Name: LC1  
    • Purpose: Identifies the first HYDRA load case.  The program will look up the temperature field corresponding to this case.  
    • Data type: Integer (load-case index)  
    • Unit: none  
    • Default: not set (must be provided by user)  

2.  T1  
    • Name: T1  
    • Purpose: Time stamp (in seconds) at which the temperature distribution for LC1 is evaluated.  
    • Data type: Real number  
    • Unit: seconds  
    • Default: not set (user-specified)  

3.  LC2  
    • Name: LC2  
    • Purpose: Identifies the second HYDRA load case for computing a temperature difference.  
    • Data type: Integer (load-case index)  
    • Unit: none  
    • Default: LC1  
      – If you omit LC2, it is assumed you want to compare LC1 to itself (see “same–case” rule below).  

4.  T2  
    • Name: T2  
    • Purpose: Time stamp (in seconds) at which the temperature distribution for LC2 is evaluated.  
    • Data type: Real number  
    • Unit: seconds  
    • Default: not set  

5.  TREF  
    • Name: TREF  
    • Purpose: Reference temperature (in °C) subtracted from the difference between the two HYDRA temperature fields.  
    • Data type: Real number  
    • Unit: degrees Celsius  
    • Default: 0.0  

**How these fields are used**  
– When you invoke TPLC, the code computes a “loading” value ΔT by  
 ΔT = T(LC2 at T2) – T(LC1 at T1) – TREF  
  where T(…) pulls the spatial temperature distribution from HYDRA’s database.  

– Special case: if LC1=LC2 (or you explicitly leave LC2 blank so it defaults to LC1), the routine automatically takes the larger of T1, T2 minus the smaller, then subtracts TREF:  
 ΔT = T(LC1 at max[T1,T2]) – T(LC1 at min[T1,T2]) – TREF  

– Immediately after TPLC is processed, all group‐factor arrays (FACT in each GRP block) are initialized to 1.0.  If you need other weighting factors, follow up with a GRP block to override those defaults.  A common pattern is to set TREF=0 in TPLC, then define your desired non-zero group factors via GRP.  

**Cross-References**  
• CTRL: overall control block of your analysis  
• GRP: used to assign element or node group load multipliers (FACT) after TPLC  
• LC: defines load-case headers in other contexts  
• PLC: pre-defined load-case collections or plates  

Storing these field descriptions in your RAG vector store will let you quickly retrieve parameter definitions, units, defaults, and usage rules when constructing or auditing HYDRA thermal load setups.

 delta T = T(LC2(T2)) - T(LC1(T1)) - TREF
 In case of LC1=LC2 always the difference between temperature distributions of larger and lower time value is computed:
 delta T = T( max(T1,T2) ) - T( min(T1,T2) ) - TREF

This table describes the GRP record, which controls how element groups participate in a given calculation step (e.g. construction-stage simulation) and how their initial (“primary”) stress state is established. Its settings apply to all load cases in the current input block. Below is a breakdown of the most important parameters and options:

1. Group Identification and Activation  
 • GRP n …  
   – Defines group number n. Elements are assigned to n either by equal-size groups (using GDIV) or by explicit lists (see SYST).  
   – If no GRP records are given, all elements are active by default. When GRP is used, only listed groups are active; others are omitted.  
   – Changing active groups causes element stiffness matrices to be reassembled.

2. Factorization Controls  
 • FACD = λd  
   – Gravity loading factor: scales self-weight (computed from material specific weight GAM/GAMA).  
 • FACS = λs  
   – Elastic-stiffness factor: scales the stiffness matrix for group elements.  
 • FACL = λl  
   – Load-case internal force factor: scales internal forces/stress state inherited from the referenced primary load case.  
 • Common relaxation use-case (tunneling): set FACD = FACS = FACL = α with 0 < α < 1.

3. Primary Load Case Reference (PLC)  
 • PLC = k  
   – References load case k as the analytical primary state for this group (defaults to global PLC).  
   – To introduce a new group with no prior load case, specify PLC = 0 or PLC = ‘SITU’.  
 • PLC = ‘SITU’  
   – Special for hardening‐plasticity soils. Deactivates hardening during this step, reaches equilibrium, then auto-calibrates internal hardening parameters to capture the true stress/strength/hardening state.

4. In-Situ Stress State Initialization  
 Two alternative procedures:  
 a) K-procedure  
   – Specify lateral earth-pressure coefficient K only. Gravity weights, SIGN/SIGH, H not used.  
 b) Analytical primary state  
   – Provide K plus GAM/GAMA, H, SIGN, and optionally SIGH.  

 Hints:  
 – You may not mix an analytical primary state with a referenced PLC primary state.  
 – Overconsolidation can be defined via OCR or pre-overburden pressure POP (see §2.4.3).  

5. Groundwater and Two-Phase (Poro-elastic) Effects  
 • HW = zw  
   – Groundwater level; elements below z w experience buoyancy using GAMA. Default HW = ∞.  
 • TYPE = UNDR / DRAI / NONP  
   – UNDR: undrained → pore-water flow suppressed → higher bulk stiffness + excess pore pressures evolve.  
   – DRAI: drained → pore-water free to flow → no stiffness contribution + existing excess pressures vanish (FACU=0).  
   – NONP: non-porous → no distinction between effective and pore pressures; NMAT.UNDR properties ignored.  
 • FACU = λu  
   – Scales initial excess pore pressure from referenced PLC. Defaults: FACU=1 for TYPE UNDR, FACU=0 for TYPE DRAI.

6. Thermal, Hydration and Swelling Loads  
 • TPLC  
   – Imports a temperature field from HYDRA (thermal load case). Use FACT=1.0.  
 • HPLC lc ALP0 alpha0  
   – References a hydration‐analysis load case (lc) and lower stiffness threshold alpha0 to vary stiffness with hydration degree.  
 • PLQ = q and FACQ = λq  
   – Swelling load case (PLQ) and swelling factor (FACQ). FACQ≠0 activates the swelling process if NMAT.SWEL is defined.

7. Hinge Deactivation  
 • HING = OFF/ON  
   – Deactivates previously defined beam hinges (both explicit and implicit) for this group.

The input table specifies the keyword parameters available when using the LCC (Load Case Copy) command to clone loads from one load case into another within the solver’s database. In LCC, all loads—except the predefined gravity loads DLX through DLZ—are transferred from a source load case to the active load case. Users may apply a uniform multiplier to those loads and restrict the copying operation either to specific elements (by group) or to a subset of nodes (by number range).

Overall Table Structure  
• Columns  
  – Item: the name of the LCC parameter  
  – Description: concise explanation of what the parameter controls  
  – Unit: physical unit or “–” if dimensionless  
  – Default: the value assumed if the user omits this parameter  

• Purpose  
  – To document the mandatory and optional parameters for LCC, their default behaviors, and usage notes.  
  – To support indexation in a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) vector store, enabling semantic search on “how to copy loads,” “applying load factors,” and “filtering nodal or element loads.”

Detailed Parameter Breakdown  
1. NO  
   • Description: Identifier (integer) of an already defined load case from which loads will be copied.  
   • Unit: — (dimensionless integer index).  
   • Default: ! (exclamation mark indicates this is required; no default exists).  
   • Remarks: Specifying NO is mandatory; it tells the solver which existing load case contains the source loads.

2. FAKT  
   • Description: Scalar multiplier applied to each load during the copy operation.  
   • Unit: — (dimensionless).  
   • Default: 1.0  
   • Remarks: A factor of 1.0 reproduces loads exactly; use values >1 to amplify or <1 to attenuate loads. Once stored, loads appear as resultants, and the original FAKT cannot be retrieved.

3. NOG  
   • Description: Element group number—only loads assigned to this element group will be copied.  
   • Unit: — (dimensionless group index).  
   • Default: – (blank means copy all element loads unless FAKT or NO filters apply).  
   • Remarks: Use in conjunction with predefined element groups to selectively merge only certain element‐based load definitions.

4. NFRO  
   • Description: Smallest node number in the range; defines the lower bound for nodal‐load copying.  
   • Unit: — (dimensionless node index).  
   • Default: – (if omitted, no lower bound is enforced when selecting nodal loads).  
   • Remarks: Together with NTO and NINC, this allows copying only a subsequence of node loads.

5. NTO  
   • Description: Largest node number in the range; defines the upper bound for nodal‐load copying.  
   • Unit: — (dimensionless node index).  
   • Default: NFRO (if NTO is omitted while NFRO is given, only the single node NFRO is selected).  
   • Remarks: Ensures a closed interval [NFRO, NTO] for selecting nodes.

6. NINC  
   • Description: Increment (step size) for node‐number iteration when copying nodal loads.  
   • Unit: — (dimensionless).  
   • Default: 1  
   • Remarks: A value of 1 copies every node in the specified range. Larger increments skip nodes (e.g., NINC = 2 copies every other node).

Contextual Notes  
– All numeric parameters are stored internally as resultants; any proportional scaling via FAKT becomes “baked in” and cannot later be decoupled.  
– The three nodal‐load parameters (NFRO, NTO, NINC) work together: omitting NFRO/NTO implies no nodal filter; omitting NINC defaults to 1.  
– The element‐filter parameter NOG can be used alone (to copy only one element group’s loads) or combined with NFRO/NTO/NINC (to further restrict nodal‐load copying).  
– This LCC functionality complements the LC command, which defines load cases from first principles; LCC streamlines reuse and combination of existing load definitions.

It appears in the “3.12 HIST – Iteration History Monitoring” section and uses four columns—Item, Description, Unit and Default—to document each keyword. Below is a detailed breakdown of its contents:

1. Column headings  
   • Item: the exact keyword you type on the input line.  
   • Description: a brief English explanation of what the keyword controls or represents.  
   • Unit: the physical dimension associated with the value (if any). A dash (—) indicates “not applicable” or a dimensionless entry.  
   • Default: the value assumed if the keyword is omitted. A dash (–) here means no default exists and the entry is mandatory.

2. Keyword “TYPE”  
   • Purpose: Selects which scalar quantity on a node will be monitored and written to the iteration history.  
   • Allowed sub-options (illustrated by “UX” in the screenshot):  
       – UX  → x-direction nodal displacement  
       – UY  → y-direction nodal displacement  
       – UZ  → z-direction nodal displacement  
     (Other common options—though not shown—could include RX, RY, RZ for rotational dofs or other specialized output types supported by your solver.)  
   • Unit: — (the monitored displacement is reported in the model’s length units but the keyword itself carries no unit)  
   • Default: – (you must explicitly specify one of the valid TYPE codes)

3. Keyword “NO”  
   • Purpose: Specifies the node number at which the chosen TYPE quantity is to be recorded.  
   • Value: an integer corresponding to an existing node ID in the model database.  
   • Unit: — (node IDs are dimensionless labels)  
   • Default: – (you must provide a valid node number; no automatic choice is provided)

How it works in practice  
 When you issue a HIST command, you supply one or more TYPE/NO pairs. For each iteration step of the non-linear solver, the iteration log will append the current value of “TYPE at node NO.” For example:  
   HIST

     TYPE UY  NO 125  
 would record both the x- and y-displacement of node 125 at every iteration. Because defaults are not defined for these entries, the user must explicitly list every quantity and node to be monitored. This mechanism provides fine-grained control over what data appear in your convergence or residual logs, enabling targeted diagnostics of displacements, rotations or other nodal output during the iterative solution process.

1. Column Descriptions  
   - Item  
     The mnemonic or keyword used in the input deck (e.g. KSV). This is the handle by which AQUA refers to each parameter.  
   - Description  
     A brief human‐readable text explaining the parameter’s purpose.  
   - Unit  
     The physical unit expected, if any. A dash (–) indicates that the parameter is dimensionless or a code‐value rather than a numerical quantity.  
   - Default  
     The value assumed when the user does not explicitly supply one.

2. Row by Row

   A. KMOD  
     • Description: “unused”  
     • Unit: –  
     • Default: “–” (no value)  
     Remarks: Although reserved in the input schema, this field currently has no effect on material evaluation. It is accepted by the parser but ignored in subsequent calculations.

   B. KSV  
     • Description: “control for basis material”  
     • Unit: –  
     • Default: SL  
     Remarks: This switch tells AQUA which form of material “working law” to read in or generate from the SSLA (stress–strain) or SFLA (force–deformation) data tables. It ties directly into the NSTR keyword, which distinguishes serviceability limit state (SLS) from ultimate limit state (ULS). Depending on service vs. ultimate and whether a safety factor is applied, the code invokes one of these variants:
       – EL: linear elastic; for concrete, tension is suppressed.  
       – ELD: same as EL but with an additional material safety factor.  
       – SL: service nominal (no safety factor). Default choice.  
       – SLD: service design (with safety factor).  
       – UL: ultimate nominal (no safety factor). Equivalent to ULD when force‐type laws are used.  
       – ULD: ultimate design (with safety factor). Equivalent to UL under force‐type laws.  
       – CAL: “calculatric” mean values (i.e. deterministic mean) without safety factors.  
       – CALD: calculatric mean values with safety factors per AQUA.  
       – PL: plastic nominal response (no safety factor).  
       – PLD: plastic design response (with safety factor).  
     Note on force‐type laws (SFLA): only SL vs UL make sense; SLD = SL and ULD = UL because safety factors are not separately modeled in the force‐displacement curves.

   C. KSB  
     • Description: “unused”  
     • Unit: –  
     • Default: “–” (no value)  
     Remarks: Like KMOD, this field is currently reserved but inactive.  

3. How KSV Fits into NSTR  
   Under NSTR you specify which limit‐state (“kind of investigated material limit state”) you are targeting: serviceability (SL(x)) or ultimate (UL(x)), each either “nominal” or “design” (i.e. with safety factors). AQUA then picks the appropriate SSLA or SFLA laws. KSV is the direct control parameter for that selection. If you leave KSV at its default (SL), AQUA will assume a serviceability nominal law with no extra material safety factors. If you need design‐level results with partial factors, you would set KSV to SLD (for service) or ULD (for ultimate), or choose one of the other EL/PL/CAL variants for linear‐elastic, plastic or mean‐value studies.

NSTR
 With NSTR the kind of investigated material limit state is specified, in particular, serviceability and ultimate limit state are distinguished, here. Depending on the choice, the appropriate material working law (cf. AQUA manual, input records SSLA and SFLA) is processed for evaluation of the material response.
 Possible specifications for KSV are::
 EL linear elastic, but without tension if concrete
 ELD linear elastic with material safety factor
 SL service nominal without material safety factor
 SLD service design with material safety factor
 UL ultimate nominal without material safety factor
 ULD ultimate design with material safety factor
 CAL Calculatoric mean values
 CALD Calculatoric mean values with safety factors from AQUA
 PL plastic nominal without material safety factor
 PLD plastic design with material safety factor
 In case of force work laws (cf. AQUA: SFLA), only serviceability state and ultimate state work laws are available. Additional consideration of possible material safety factors is not accounted for, i.e., the UL and ULD statements are eqivalent in this case (the same holds for SL and SLD).

This table defines a single input parameter, PROB, which controls the basic type of analysis to be performed. It is intended to appear in the “CSYS” (coordinate system) or “SYST” (system definition) record context of a larger data file, and if specified before any stage‐by‐stage construction descriptions, its value becomes the default for all subsequent construction stages.

1. Parameter Name  
   • PROB  

2. Purpose  
   PROB determines whether the solver will carry out a purely linear analysis or a physical non-linear analysis. It effectively switches the mathematical formulation of the problem.  

3. Data Type and Units  
   • Unit: LIT (literal)  
   • Because PROB only accepts discrete text codes, it is designated as a literal (string) rather than a numeric field.  

4. Permitted Values  
   • LINE – instructs the system to perform a standard linear analysis. Under this mode, all relationships remain linear, material properties and boundary conditions are assumed not to change with the applied loads or deformations.  
   • NONL – instructs the system to perform a physical non-linear analysis. In this mode, the solver will account for effects such as large deformations, material non-linearities (plasticity, hyperelasticity, creep, etc.), contact, and other state-dependent behaviors.  

5. Default Setting  
   • NONL  
   If the user omits PROB, the system presumes a non-linear analysis by default. This choice reflects the fact that many real-world problems require at least some degree of non-linear modeling to capture accurate structural response.  

6. Interaction with CSYS/SYST Records  
   • When the CSYS record appears before any “CS” or stage-specific description (see also CS and CCRL records), PROB’s setting applies globally until it is overridden by another PROB entry.  
   • If multiple stages of a construction sequence each require different analysis types, PROB may be repeated at each stage. Otherwise, the initial PROB value persists.  

7. Cross-References  
   • See also the CS record, which defines coordinate system details for each construction stage.  
   • See CCRL for material and component reference linking.  

By consolidating the analysis type into a single flag, PROB simplifies input files and ensures consistency across multiple build stages unless explicitly changed by the user.

See also: CS, CCRL
 CSYS
 CSYS is related to record SYST - however, input requirements are reduced to a basic definition of the type of problem.
 In case CSYS is specified prior to the first CS-description, the specified settings serve as a default for all construction stages.

The table shown is the definition of the CCRL record for a staged‐construction (LSE) analysis.  CCRL lets you specify a suite of control options for all construction stages—or, when used in conjunction with the SLCT option, only a selected subset of them.  Its fields break down as follows:

1.  Column Headings  
    •  Item: the keyword of the CCRL field.  
    •  Description: what the field does or what it controls.  
    •  Unit: the physical or logical unit in which the field is interpreted.  
    •  Default: the default value if you omit that field.

2.  Rows of the Table

— PT (Unit = LIT, Default = “–”)  
   “PT” is mandatory and must be followed by one of a fixed list of literals (LIT).  It tells LSE exactly which control block you are describing.  Legal PT values include:  
     •  ITER  – iteration–control parameters  
     •  KITE  – choice of iteration method  
     •  LSRC  – line–search control  
     •  STEP  – load–stepping continuation method  
     •  EPOL  – extrapolation of first‐iteration displacements  
     •  SPRI  – spring, truss, cable elements  
     •  BEAM  – beam‐element controls  
     •  FIRE  – “hot” material laws  
     •  CONC  – concrete material parameters  
     •  TSTF  – tension‐stiffening control  
     •  GRAN  – adaptation for GRAN material law  
     •  AFIX  – automatic support‐condition generation  
     •  SOLV  – solver‐options for LSE  
     •  SLCT  – selection of active construction stages

— VAL (Unit = –, Default = “*”)  
   The primary numerical value or flag for the chosen analysis option (depending on PT).  Often used to turn an option on/off or specify a principal magnitude.

— FMAX (Unit = –, Default = “*”)  
   A first auxiliary floating‐point parameter.  Its meaning depends entirely on which PT you chose (e.g. maximum line‐search factor for LSRC, upper bound on load‐step increase for STEP, etc.).

— FMIN (Unit = –, Default = “*”)  
   A second auxiliary floating‐point parameter, used in PT blocks that require both upper and lower tolerances or bounds.

— EMAX (Unit = –, Default = “*”)  
   A third auxiliary parameter; typically a strain or error criterion when controlling convergence in nonlinear iterations.

— EMIN (Unit = –, Default = “*”)  
   A fourth auxiliary parameter that often serves as a secondary convergence threshold or safety lower‐limit.

— SAVE (Unit = –, Default = “*”)  
   The storage interval of load increments.  Controls how often LSE writes intermediate load‐increment results into the restart or output file.

3.  Contextual Notes  
— CCRL is closely linked with the global CTRL record.  For full details on what each parameter literally does under the hood, you should cross‐reference the “CTRL” documentation.  
— If you place a CCRL before any CS (construction stage) descriptions, its settings become the default for every stage that follows—saving you from having to repeat common controls.  
— When you use PT=SLCT, you can activate only a subset of construction stages; the others are skipped entirely (no calculation or output).

4.  How to Use this Table in Practice  
— Start each CCRL record with “CCRL PT=xxx” where “xxx” is one of the literals above.  
— Supply at least VAL (or leave it “*” to inherit defaults).  
— Supply FMAX/FMIN/EMAX/EMIN only if that PT block actually needs them (refer to CTRL for which blocks do).  
— Optionally set SAVE if you want to tweak how often load‐increments are stored.  
— Group multiple CCRL records to customize different aspects of the LSE solution—e.g. one CCRL for “PT=ITER” to tune convergence, another for “PT=STEP” to control stepping, and so on.

The table defines the SLCT (select) record, which is used to activate only a specified sub-range of construction stages (CS) when running an analysis. Any stages outside the selected range are not computed, printed or otherwise processed once SLCT is in effect. This mechanism can be combined with other related records (see CS, CSYS and CTRL) or with the CCRL record (for saved load-increment storage intervals) to establish defaults and fine-tune which construction stages are actually executed. If CCRL appears before any CS descriptions, its settings act as defaults for all subsequent construction stages.  

Key Fields in the SLCT Record  
1. VAL  
   • Description: “First active construction stage CS.”  
   • Purpose: Specifies the index or identifier of the very first construction stage that the solver should actively process. All CS numbers below this value are suppressed (their computations may be skipped and their output not generated).  
   • Unit: None (this is a unitless integer index).  
   • Default: 0 (by default, no lower bound is imposed, so processing starts at CS 0 unless overridden).  

2. FMAX  
   • Description: “Final construction stage CS of the active sequence.”  
   • Purpose: Sets an upper bound on which construction stage will be executed. Any stage whose CS number exceeds this value will not be computed. The solver effectively stops generating new stages once it reaches FMAX.  
   • Unit: None (integer index).  
   • Default: ∞ (infinite)—meaning by default there is no upper cut-off and all stages up to the last defined CS are processed.  

3. FMIN  
   • Description: “Mode for inactive construction stages.”  
   • Purpose: Controls how the solver treats CS indices that lie outside the [VAL, FMAX] range. Two sub-options are available:  
     – 0: Inactive construction stage controls are still printed in the output, but all related parameters and solution components are set inactive. This corresponds internally to “–PROG TALPA” behavior.  
     – –1: Printing of inactive construction stage controls is fully suppressed—no trace of those stages appears in the output or log. They are completely ignored.  
   • Unit: None (mode flag).  
   • Default: 0 (by default, out-of-range stages are printed but inactivated rather than fully hidden).  

How SLCT Interacts with Other Records  
• If you need to save only certain stages’ state or results, you would pair SLCT with CCRL (SAVE Storage interval of load increments). CCRL may inherit defaults from SLCT if CCRL appears earlier.  
• For detailed control of what each CS does—such as boundary conditions, loading, or material changes—you would still use CS and CSYS records in combination with CTRL options. SLCT simply gates which CS definitions actually get executed at all.  
• By setting VAL > 0 or FMAX < ∞, you can effectively resume an analysis at an intermediate stage or run only a subset of a full construction sequence for faster iterations or parametric studies.  

In practice, the SLCT record allows engineers to isolate and run only the meaningful portion of a construction sequence, suppressing setup or final stages as needed, while retaining the ability to document inactivated stages or hide them entirely from output. This is particularly useful in large parametric studies or when re-running analyses from mid-point.

See also: CS, CSYS, CTRL
 CCRL
 SAVE Storage interval of load increments

The table summarizes the syntax and semantics of the CS (Construction Stage) record, which marks the beginning of a new construction‐stage description in a staged‐construction model. Each row of the table corresponds to one field (or subfield) of CS; the four columns define (1) the field name (“Item”), (2) its meaning (“Description”), (3) the units or data type (“Unit”), and (4) any assumed default value if the field is omitted (“Default”). Below is a guided walkthrough of each field and how it links into the overall staged‐construction logic.

1. NO  – Construction Stage Number  
   • Description: A unique identifier for this construction stage.  
   • Unit/Data Type: “–” (integer, but no physical unit).  
   • Default: none (must be supplied or auto–assigned).  
   • Notes: If omitted, the program auto-numbers stages in ascending order. Manually assigned numbers must also increase; illegal numbering triggers an automatic renumbering.

2. DT  – Duration of Construction Stage  
   • Description: The time span over which this stage is active. This feeds into any time‐dependent material or structural modelling.  
   • Unit: seconds ([sec]₁₂₉₀).  
   • Default: none (required when time dependence matters).

3. PCS  – Preceding Construction Stage  
   • Description: A reference to another stage whose state will serve as the “base” or “reference” for this one.  
   • Unit/Data Type: “–” (integer index).  
   • Default: “*”  
     – “*” signals the immediately previous stage in sequence.  
   • Notes: Overriding the default lets you branch: e.g. refer back two stages or to any earlier one to define a non-linear build sequence.

4. DEFO  – Deformation of Preceding Construction Stage  
   • Description: Controls how displacements from the previous stage combine with any new displacement increments. Two options:  
     • INC  
       – Store only the *incremental* displacement of the current stage. The earlier total deformation is ignored when post-processing.  
     • FULL  
       – Store the *cumulative* displacement (previous total plus new increment).  
   • Unit/Data Type: “–” (enumeration INC|FULL).  
   • Default: FULL

5. TITL  – Title of Construction Stage  
   • Description: A short text descriptor (up to 30 characters) for user reference or summary listings.  
   • Unit/Data Type: LIT (literal string).  
   • Default: none

How This Fits into the RAG Workflow  
• The CS record by itself contains only high-level metadata (stage number, duration, link to prior stage, storage mode, and a human‐readable title).  
• The actual physical changes—adding or removing elements, applying loads or boundary conditions—are detailed in subsequent specifications (CGRP for group definitions, CLOA for load assignments, CGW for element removal, etc.).  
• By chaining CS records in the input file, the user constructs a timeline of incremental changes. Each stage automatically inherits the geometry and state of its “preceding” stage, unless a different PCS is explicitly specified.  
• This staged logic drastically reduces input effort: only *changes* need to be declared in each stage, and deformation history is handled by the DEFO flag.

See also: CGRP, CSYS, CCRL
 CS
 Record CS initiates a construction stage description. It only contains general descriptors that relate to the construction stage as a whole (cs-number, duration, labelling). The actual specifi- cation of what happens during this construction phase results from subsequent CGRP, CLOA and CGW specifications. Sequence of construction stages in the input specification corre- sponds to the actual construction sequence. Therefore, construction stage description is lim- ited to indication of changes with respect to the foregoing construction phase - e.g. removal of an element group from the system -which reduces input effort significantly (→ CGRP, CLOA, CGW).
 If no construction stage number is specified, numbering is performed automatically. With man- ual assignment, assure that numbering is in ascending order. In case of illegal numbering the program switches to automatic assignment.
 Duration of the construction phase is among other things relevant for modelling of time depen- dent material characteristics.
 As described above, the construction stage specification reflects the logic of a staged construc- tion sequence: the reference state for each construction stage is defined by the description of the preceeding one. This default behaviour can be overridden by PCS referring to an arbitrary, previously defined construction stage number.

The table shown is the specification of the CGRP record, which defines how an element group is handled in a particular construction stage.  In a RAG/vector‐store context, each row of this table represents one input field (or “item”) you can index for retrieval.  Below is a field‐by‐field breakdown:

1.  NO  
 – Description: Group number (integer) or keyword ALL to apply to every group.  
 – Unit: “–” (no physical unit; literal)  
 – Default: mandatory (indicated by “!”)  

2.  ACT  
 – Description: Primary action code for this group.  One of:  
  • SITU  – compute in-situ stresses (evaluate K, HW, MNO, PTSZ, TYPE)  
  • RLX   – perform relaxation (alpha-method; evaluate ALPH, HW, PTSZ, TYPE)  
  • EX    – excavate/remove the group  
  • IN    – install the group (evaluate FAKS, HW, PTYP, MNO, PTSZ, TYPE)  
  • PRE   – prestressing placeholder (not yet active)  
  • MODI  – modify group properties (evaluate FAKS, HW, MNO, PLQ, PTSZ, TYPE)  
 – Unit: “LIT” (literal string)  
 – Default: MODI  

3.  ACT2  
 – Description: Supplemental action flag, controls output formatting.  
  • FULL – group is active, full printed output  
  • LINE – group is linear, printed output only line-by-line  
 – Unit: “LIT”  
 – Default: FULL  

4.  FAKS  
 – Description: Stiffness factor for group (scales stiffness matrix)  
 – Unit: “–” (dimensionless)  
 – Default: 1.0  

5.  ALPH  
 – Description: Alpha-relaxation factor (for RLX actions)  
 – Unit: “–”  
 – Default: 1.0  

6.  HW  
 – Description: Elevation of groundwater level (ordinate)  
 – Unit: meters [m]  
 – Default: unset (“–”)  

7.  K  
 – Description: Lateral earth pressure coefficient in primary state (for SITU)  
 – Unit: “–”  
 – Default: mandatory (“!”)  

8.  OCR  
 – Description: Over-Consolidation Ratio (soil parameter)  
 – Unit: “–”  
 – Default: none (“–”)  

9.  POP  
 – Description: Pre-overburden pressure (at reference depth)  
 – Unit: kilonewton per square meter [kN/m²]  
 – Default: none (“–”)  

10.  P  
 – Description: Prestressing force (not yet available/apply when PRE is used)  
 – Unit: kilonewton [kN]  
 – Default: mandatory (“!”)  

11.  PTYP  
 – Description: Prestressing type, one of:  
  • FFIN – P is final force in the structural member  
  • FINI – P is initial force; final force emerges from structural response  
 – Unit: “LIT”  
 – Default: FFIN  

12.  PLQ  
 – Description: Primary load case for swelling analysis (used in MODI)  
 – Unit: “–”  
 – Default: none (“–”)  

13.  MNO  
 – Description: Material number reference (links to material database)  
 – Unit: “–”  
 – Default: none (“–”)  

14.  PTSZ  
 – Description: Number of cross-sectional fibers (fiber beam elements only)  
 – Unit: “–”  
 – Default: see CTRL (controlled elsewhere)  

15.  TYPE  
 – Description: Two‐phase model selection (continuum elements only).  Choose:  
  • NONP – non-porous material (single-phase model)  
  • DRAI – drained, pore-flow allowed  
  • UNDR – undrained, pore-flow suppressed  
 – Unit: “–”  
 – Default: NONP  

Context and Usage Notes:  
•  CGRP records are only required for groups whose status changes relative to the previous construction stage (installation, removal, modification, stress‐state initialization, etc.).  Unchanged groups inherit the prior stage’s settings automatically.  
•  The ACT code determines which of the supplementary fields (K, OCR, POP, FAKS, ALPH, PTYP, etc.) must be supplied and how they are interpreted.  
•  SITU and RLX actions both compute or relax the in-situ stress state; EX and IN handle excavation versus erection; MODI updates any combination of stiffness, groundwater, material, prestress or swelling parameters.  
•  Together with the related CS (Construction Stage) and CSYS/CCRL records, CGRP fully defines the staged application of loads, boundary conditions, pore‐pressure settings and material changes in a geotechnical or structural simulation.

See also: CS, CSYS, CCRL
